title: Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to the Threat From Securities Investments That Finance Certain Companies of the People's Republic of China
full_text:
(

Notice of November 3, 2026
Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to the Threat From Securities Investments That Finance Certain Companies of the People's Republic of China
On November 12, 2020, by
Executive Order 13959
, the President declared a national emergency pursuant to the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (
50 U.S.C. 1701
et seq.
) to deal with the unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States constituted by the threat from securities investments that finance certain companies of the People's Republic of China (PRC).
The President found that the PRC is increasingly exploiting United States capital to resource and enable the development and modernization of its military, intelligence, and other security apparatuses, which continues to allow the PRC to directly threaten the United States homeland and United States forces overseas. Through the national strategy of Military-Civil Fusion, the PRC increases the size of the country's military-industrial complex by compelling civilian Chinese companies to support its military and intelligence activities. Those companies, though remaining ostensibly private and civilian, directly support the PRC's military, intelligence, and security apparatuses and aid in their development and modernization. At the same time, those companies raise capital by selling securities to United States investors that trade on public exchanges both here and abroad, lobbying United States index providers and funds to include these securities in market offerings, and engaging in other acts to ensure access to United States capital.
The President further found that the PRC's military-industrial complex, by directly supporting the efforts of the PRC's military, intelligence, and other security apparatuses, constituted an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States.
On January 13, 2021, the President signed
Executive Order 13974
amending
Executive Order 13959
.
On June 3, 2021, the President signed
Executive Order 14032
, which expanded the scope of the national emergency declared in
Executive Order 13959
. The President found that additional steps were necessary to address that national emergency, including the threat posed by the military-industrial complex of the PRC and its involvement in military, intelligence, and security research and development programs, and weapons and related equipment production under the PRC's Military-Civil Fusion strategy. In addition, the President found that the use of Chinese surveillance technology outside the PRC and the development or use of Chinese surveillance technology to facilitate repression or serious human rights abuse constituted unusual and extraordinary threats to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States.
Executive Order 14032
amended
Executive Order 13959
and revoked
Executive Order 13974
in its entirety.
The threat from securities investments that finance certain companies of the PRC and certain uses and development of Chinese surveillance technology continue to pose an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States.
For this reason, the national emergency declared in
Executive Order 13959
of November 12, 2020, expanded in scope by
Executive Order 14032
of
(
printed page 69954)
June 3, 2021, must continue in effect beyond November 12, 2026. Therefore, in accordance with section 202(d) of the National Emergencies Act (
50 U.S.C. 1622(d)
), I am continuing for 1 year the national emergency declared in
Executive Order 13959
with respect to the threat from securities investments that finance certain companies of the PRC and expanded in
Executive Order 14032
.
This notice shall be published in the
Federal Register
and transmitted to the Congress.
THE WHITE HOUSE,
November 3, 2026.

Notice of November 3, 2026
Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to the Situation in Nicaragua
On November 27, 2018, by
Executive Order 13851
, the President declared a national emergency pursuant to the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (
50 U.S.C. 1701
et seq.
) to deal with the unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and foreign policy of the United States constituted by the situation in Nicaragua. On October 24, 2022, the President issued
Executive Order 14088
to take additional steps with respect to the national emergency declared in
Executive Order 13851
.
The situation in Nicaragua, including the violent response by the Government of Nicaragua to the protests that began on April 18, 2018, and the Ortega-Murillo regime's continued systematic dismantling and undermining of democratic institutions and the rule of law, its use of indiscriminate violence and repressive tactics against civilians, as well as its corruption leading to the destabilization of Nicaragua's economy, continues to pose an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security and foreign policy of the United States. For this reason, the national emergency declared on November 27, 2018, must continue in effect beyond November 27, 2026. Therefore, in accordance with section 202(d) of the National Emergencies Act (
50 U.S.C. 1622(d)
), I am continuing for 1 year the national emergency declared in
Executive Order 13851
with respect to the situation in Nicaragua.
This notice shall be published in the
Federal Register
and transmitted to the Congress.
THE WHITE HOUSE,
November 3, 2026.

Notice of November 3, 2026
Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to the Proliferation of Weapons of Mass Destruction
On November 14, 1994, by
Executive Order 12938
, the President declared a national emergency with respect to the unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States posed by the proliferation of nuclear, biological, and chemical weapons (weapons of mass destruction) and the means of delivering such weapons. On July 28, 1998, by
Executive Order 13094
, the President amended
Executive Order 12938
to respond more effectively to the worldwide threat of proliferation activities related to weapons of mass destruction. On June 28, 2005, by
Executive Order 13382
, the President, among other things, further amended
Executive Order 12938
to improve our ability to combat proliferation activities related to weapons of mass destruction. The proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and the means of delivering them continues to pose an unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States. For this reason, the national emergency declared in
Executive Order 12938
with respect to the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and the means of delivering such weapons must continue beyond November 14, 2026. Therefore, in accordance with section 202(d) of the National Emergencies Act (
50 U.S.C. 1622(d)
), I am continuing for 1 year the national emergency declared in
Executive Order 12938
, as amended.
This notice shall be published in the
Federal Register
and transmitted to the Congress.

title: Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to Iran
full_text:
Notice of November 3, 2026
Continuation of the National Emergency With Respect to Iran
On November 14, 1979, by
Executive Order 12170
, the President declared a national emergency with respect to Iran pursuant to the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (
50 U.S.C. 1701
et seq.
) and took related steps to deal with the unusual and extraordinary threat to the national security, foreign policy, and economy of the United States constituted by the situation in Iran.
Our relations with Iran have not yet normalized, and the process of implementing the agreements with Iran, dated January 19, 1981, is ongoing. For this reason, the national emergency declared on November 14, 1979, and the measures adopted on that date to deal with that emergency, must continue in effect beyond November 14, 2026. Therefore, in accordance with section 202(d) of the National Emergencies Act (
50 U.S.C. 1622(d)
), I am continuing for 1 year the national emergency with respect to Iran declared in
Executive Order 12170
.
The emergency declared by
Executive Order 12170
is distinct from the emergency declared in
Executive Order 12957
on March 15, 1995. This renewal, therefore, is distinct from the emergency renewal of March 2, 2026.
This notice shall be published in the
Federal Register
and transmitted to the Congress.
THE WHITE HOUSE,
November 3, 2026.

Legal Services Corporation
45 CFR Part 1631
AGENCY:
Legal Services Corporation.
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking.
SUMMARY:
This proposed rule revises the Legal Services Corporation's (LSC) definition of “capital improvement” by removing the threshold amount of LSC funds that must be expended on an improvement to real estate for the expenditure to qualify as a capital improvement. The proposed amendment would distinguish the definition of a capital improvement from the monetary thresholds required for prior approval; promote consistent tracking and oversight of LSC funds used for capital improvements; and strengthen accountability for LSC funds invested in recipients' real property.
DATES:
Comments must be submitted by 11:59 p.m. Eastern on December 21, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by any of the following methods:
Email:
lscrulemaking@lsc.gov
.
Include “Comments on Revision to Part 1631” in the subject line of the message.
Mail:
Brittany Sims Nwankwoala, Assistant General Counsel, Legal Services Corporation, 1825 I St. NW, Ste. 800, Washington, DC 20006, ATTN: Part 1631 Rulemaking.
(
printed page 69767)
Hand Delivery/Courier:
Brittany Sims Nwankwoala, Assistant General Counsel, Legal Services Corporation, 1825 I St. NW, Ste. 800, Washington, DC 20006, ATTN: Part 1631 Rulemaking.
Instructions:
Electronic submissions are preferred via email with attachments in Acrobat PDF format. LSC will not consider written comments sent to any other address or received after the end of the comment period.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Brittany Sims Nwankwoala, Assistant General Counsel, Legal Services Corporation, 1825 I St. NW, Ste. 800, Washington, DC 20006; (202) 295-1599 (phone), or
nwankwoalab@lsc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The Legal Services Corporation Act of 1974 authorizes LSC to establish regulations governing the use of grant funds and to ensure appropriate stewardship of Federal resources. See
42 U.S.C. 2996g(e)
. LSC sets forth its procurement and property management requirements in
45 CFR part 1631
.
In 2017, LSC revised parts 1630, pertaining to cost standards, and 1631 to increase the prior approval threshold from $10,000 to $25,000 to account for inflation and reduce unnecessary administrative burdens on recipients. This change also established $25,000 as the applicable threshold in all provisions governing prior approval, property, and procurement requirements. In 2022, LSC conducted a retrospective review of all regulations. It identified several additional areas within parts 1630 and 1631 that recipients and LSC staff found difficult to administer consistently or that lacked sufficient clarity for grantees and oversight staff. In 2026, LSC initiated rulemaking to resolve those inconsistencies and increase the $25,000 prior approval threshold to $50,000 in §§ 1630.3, 1630.6, 1631.8, and 1631.15. See
91 FR 23228
(Apr. 30, 2026).
During the 2026 rulemaking, however, LSC did not propose increasing the threshold in the definition of “capital improvement” in § 1631.2(a). Although LSC increased the threshold for obtaining prior approval for certain expenditures from $25,000 to $50,000, that amendment would not address which expenditures constitute capital improvements for purposes of part 1631. Rather, through subsequent conversations with the Office of Compliance Enforcement (OCE), LSC found that removing the threshold amount altogether would enhance LSC's ability to identify and account for all LSC funds used to improve real property. Currently, expenditures below the threshold may nevertheless constitute capital improvements and, when repeatedly made over time, could represent a significant investment of LSC funds in a recipient's real property. The $50,000 threshold for determining when prior approval is required remains separate from the definition of “capital improvement.”
II. Remove the Threshold Amount in Definition of Capital Improvement
LSC proposes to revise the definition of “capital improvement” in § 1631.2(a) by removing any monetary threshold from the definition. Currently, § 1631.2(a) defines “capital improvement” as spending more than $50,000 of LSC funds to improve real estate through construction or the addition of fixtures that become an integral part of the real estate. LSC proposes to remove the monetary threshold so that any improvement to real estate using LSC funds constitutes a capital improvement.
LSC is undertaking this rulemaking to strengthen its oversight of LSC funds used to improve real property and ensure that recipients identify and account for such expenditures regardless of amount. The amendment also clarifies that an expenditure may constitute a capital improvement even if it does not meet the monetary threshold requiring LSC's prior approval. The character of an expenditure made with LSC funds as a capital improvement does not depend on its cost. An expenditure may improve real estate through construction or the addition of an integral fixture even when the amount of LSC funds used for that particular improvement is less than the applicable prior approval threshold.
Removing the monetary threshold from the definition would also ensure that recipients identify and account for any LSC funds used for capital improvements regardless of the amount of the individual expenditure. Under the current definition, improvements costing less than $50,000 do not constitute “capital improvements” for purposes of part 1631. As a result, a recipient could make multiple improvements to the same real estate over time using LSC funds, with each individual improvement falling below $50,000, without those expenditures being treated as capital improvements under the rule. For example, a recipient could expend $30,000 of LSC funds on an improvement in one year and later expend an additional $40,000 on another improvement to the same property in a different year. Although the recipient would have invested a total of $70,000 of LSC funds in improvements to the property, neither expenditure would constitute a capital improvement under the current definition.
This result is inconsistent with LSC's interest in ensuring that recipients accurately identify and account for LSC funds invested in real estate. Section 1631.15(c) requires recipients to maintain supporting documentation sufficient to accurately identify and account for any use of LSC funds to make capital improvements to real estate owned by the recipient. Removing the $50,000 threshold from the definition would make the definition consistent with that requirement and enable LSC and recipients to account for the cumulative amount of LSC funds invested in improvements to real estate over time.
The proposed amendment would also clarify the distinction between the classification and tracking of an expenditure and the requirement to obtain prior approval. Removing the dollar amount from the definition of “capital improvement” would not, by itself, require prior approval for every capital improvement. Rather, grantees would need to treat and track expenditures that meet the definition as a capital improvement regardless of amount. Meanwhile, the applicable provisions governing prior approval would continue to determine when a recipient must obtain LSC's approval before using LSC funds for the improvement.
This change would ensure that the regulatory definition accurately identifies the nature of the expenditure and that LSC's interest in real estate reflects LSC funds used for capital improvements, including improvements made through multiple expenditures over time.
IV. Proposed Changes
PART 1631—PURCHASING AND PROPERTY MANAGEMENT
§ 1631.2
Definitions
LSC proposes to revise the definition of “capital improvement” in § 1631.2(a) by removing the monetary amount of LSC funds a recipient may spend to improve real property through construction or the addition of fixtures that become an integral part of the real property.
List of Subjects in
45 CFR Part 1631
Government contracts
Grant programs—law
Legal services
Real property acquisition
(
printed page 69768)
For the reasons set forth in the preamble, the Legal Services Corporation proposes to amend
part 1631 of title 45 of the Code of Federal Regulations
as follows:
PART 1631—PURCHASING AND PROPERTY MANAGEMENT
1.
The authority citation for part 1631 continues to read as follows:
Authority:
42 U.S.C. 2996g(e)
.
2.
Amend § 1631.2 by revising paragraph (a) to read as follows:
§ 1631.2.
Definitions.
(a) Capital improvement means spending any amount of LSC funds to improve real estate through construction or the addition of fixtures that become an integral part of real estate.

Legal Services Corporation
45 CFR Parts 1630 and 1631
AGENCY:
Legal Services Corporation.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule revises the Legal Services Corporation's (LSC or Corporation) regulations governing cost allowability, prior approval requirements, and property and procurement standards applicable to LSC recipients. The final rule clarifies when recipients must obtain prior approval for expenditures of LSC funds; increases the monetary threshold for prior approval; clarifies the treatment of proceeds from fundraising activities supported with LSC funds; provides additional flexibility in LSC's review of prior approval requests; clarifies documentation requirements for prior approval requests; and revises the deadline and requirements for accounting for LSC funds invested in real estate. These amendments are intended to clarify existing requirements, reduce administrative burden, promote consistent oversight and enforcement, and strengthen accountability in the use of Federal funds.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on June 1, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Brittany Sims Nwankwoala, Assistant General Counsel, Legal Services Corporation, 1825 I St. NW, Ste. 800, Washington, DC 20006; (202) 295-1599 (phone), or
nwankwoalab@lsc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
The Legal Services Corporation Act of 1974 authorizes LSC to establish regulations governing the use of grant funds and to ensure appropriate stewardship of Federal resources. See
42 U.S.C. 2996g(e)
. LSC sets forth its cost standards and prior approval requirements in
45 CFR part 1630
and its procurement and property management requirements in
45 CFR part 1631
.
LSC last revised part 1630 in 2017 to provide uniform standards governing the allowability and allocation of costs charged to LSC grants and contracts. Among other things, the 2017 rule required costs to be actually incurred, reasonable and necessary, allocable to the grant or contract, consistent with generally accepted accounting principles and recipient accounting practices, and adequately documented. The 2017 rule also established requirements governing prior written approval and questioned cost proceedings. As part of that rulemaking, LSC increased the prior approval threshold from $10,000 to $25,000 to account for inflation.
(
printed page 69721)
During the same rulemaking, LSC incorporated its property acquisition and management policies into the Code of Federal Regulations as
45 CFR part 1631
. Part 1631 establishes standards for purchasing, leasing, using, and disposing of LSC-funded personal property and real estate and for using LSC funds to contract for services.
In 2022, LSC conducted a retrospective review of its regulations to determine whether existing provisions remained clear, effective, and aligned with current programmatic and compliance realities. That review identified several provisions in parts 1630 and 1631 that recipients and LSC staff found difficult to administer consistently or that lacked sufficient clarity for recipients and oversight staff. Subsequent discussions with the Office of Compliance and Enforcement, the Office of Inspector General (OIG), and other internal stakeholders confirmed those concerns.
LSC determined that regulatory action was appropriate to address ambiguities in its cost standards, prior approval requirements, and property and procurement regulations that had resulted in inconsistent interpretation and application. Since LSC last substantively revised parts 1630 and 1631 in 2017, changes in recipient operations, procurement practices, and fiscal environments have exposed limitations in the existing regulatory framework that guidance alone cannot resolve.
II. Procedural History of This Rulemaking
On January 22, 2026, the Operations and Regulations Committee (Committee) of LSC's Board of Directors (Board) voted to recommend that the Board authorize LSC to engage in rulemaking on parts 1630 and 1631. On January 27, 2026, the Board accepted the Committee's recommendation and authorized LSC to engage in rulemaking.
On March 19, 2026, the Committee voted to recommend that the Board authorize publication of a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM). On March 23, 2026, the Board voted to authorize LSC to publish the NPRM for notice and comment.
On April 30, 2026, LSC published the NPRM in the
Federal Register
.
91 FR 23228
, Apr. 30, 2026. LSC sought public comment on LSC's proposed revisions concerning the prior approval threshold and timing requirements, fundraising proceeds, review timelines for prior approval requests, documentation supporting prior approval requests, and accounting for LSC funds invested in real estate. The comment period closed on June 29, 2026.
Materials regarding this rulemaking are available in the open rulemaking section of LSC's website at
https://www.lsc.gov/​about-lsc/​laws-regulations-and-guidance/​rulemaking
. After the effective date of the rule, those materials will appear in the closed rulemaking section at
https://www.lsc.gov/​about-lsc/​laws-regulations-and-guidance/​rulemaking/​closed-rulemaking
.
III. Discussion of Comments and Regulatory Provisions
LSC received three comments during the public comments period: (1) the National Legal Aid and Defender Association (NLADA); (2) Community Legal Services located in Orlando, Florida, an LSC funding recipient; and (3) James E. Scarborough, an individual contributor. All commenters expressed support for several elements of the proposed revisions to parts 1630 and 1631.
NLADA stated that it supported LSC's proposal to raise the prior approval threshold to $50,000, which they stated would help reduce low-risk administrative burdens. They also supported the plan to provide greater flexibility in accounting deadlines tied to recipients' audited financial statements. Additionally, NLADA requested that LSC further clarify the fundraising reimbursement rule to define what counts as “fundraising costs” and to exclude all staff salaries from that definition to avoid impractical tracking burdens and unintended inefficiencies.
Jeffrey D. Harvey, CEO of Community Legal Services in Orlando, FL, requested additional clarification on how the proposed standard for recipients to obtain prior approval before they incur a legal obligation to expend LSC funds applies to recurring or month-to-month contracts, allocation changes over time, and whether these situations trigger prior approval under the new rule.
James E. Scarborough supported LSC's efforts to reduce administrative burden and clarify requirements. He asked LSC to provide stronger justification for the proposed $50,000 prior-approval threshold, consider alternative approaches, and offer additional implementation guidance for the revised fundraising and accounting provisions.
IV. Section-by-Section Discussion of Proposed Changes and Comments
A. Part 1630—Cost Standards and Procedures
§ 1630.5 Standards Governing Allowability of Costs Under LSC Grants or Contracts
LSC proposed to revise § 1630.5(i) to clarify the treatment of proceeds from fundraising activities supported in whole or in part with LSC funds. LSC added § 1630.5(i) in 2017 to codify its longstanding policy permitting recipients to use LSC funds for allowable fundraising activities undertaken to increase the resources available to carry out the purposes of an LSC grant. OIG urged LSC to require recipients to treat fundraising proceeds as derivative income or, alternatively, to require recipients to reimburse the LSC account for allowable fundraising costs before allocating the remaining proceeds to other accounts.
LSC has determined that fundraising proceeds should not be included in the definition of derivative income. The definition of derivative income adopted in the 1997 final rule limits that term to income generated by activities directly supported by Federal grant funds and excludes grants, contracts, or contributions from non-LSC sources. Furthermore, LSC has determined that proceeds generated through fundraising are not “earned” within the meaning of derivative income. Unlike costs incurred in the ordinary course of business operations, fundraising expenses are distinctly different; they are incurred for the purpose of soliciting contributions and do not transform those contributions into earned income. Similarly, gifts are not considered earned income. Treating fundraising proceeds as derivative income would be inconsistent with that framework
Comments:
NLADA requested clarification regarding what constitutes a “fundraising cost” subject to the proposed reimbursement requirement. NLADA agreed that reimbursement is reasonable when LSC funds are used for costs directly associated with a fundraising activity, such as venue/space rental fees, food, or other expenses associated with planning and hosting a fundraising event. NLADA expressed concern, however, that the proposed language could be interpreted to include staff salaries, efforts to secure grants, and costs associated with creating promotional or educational materials. NLADA stated that such an interpretation could require recipients to track and retrospectively allocate staff time and other ordinary operating costs
(
printed page 69722)
whenever those activities ultimately contribute to successful fundraising. NLADA also noted that restrictions applicable to another grant may prevent a recipient from using the proceeds of that grant to reimburse its LSC account. NLADA therefore requested that LSC clarify what constitutes a fundraising cost or identify costs that are not subject to the reimbursement requirement. James Scarborough similarly recommended that LSC provide implementation guidance or examples concerning the treatment of fundraising proceeds
Response:
LSC Management agrees that clarification is appropriate. LSC intends the reimbursement requirement to apply to costs directly attributable to a fundraising activity for which the recipient receives fundraising proceeds. For example, if a recipient uses LSC funds to pay for venue/space, food, printing, or other costs incurred specifically to conduct a fundraising event, the recipient must reimburse its LSC account from the proceeds of that activity in an amount equal to the LSC funds used for those costs. LSC does not intend the provision to require recipients to identify and reimburse ordinary personnel, administrative, outreach, or educational costs merely because those activities or materials subsequently contribute to fundraising. Similarly, the provision does not require reimbursement for the costs of staff salaries incurred in preparing grant applications. Nor does LSC intend to require a recipient to use the proceeds of a grant or contribution in a manner inconsistent with restrictions imposed by the source of those funds. The relevant inquiry is whether the cost was incurred specifically for the fundraising activity rather than whether an activity or work product ultimately contributed to the recipient's ability to obtain non-LSC funds.
LSC believes this interpretation addresses NLADA's concerns while effectuating the purpose of the amendment. The final rule therefore retains the proposed reimbursement requirement. LSC provides this explanation to clarify the scope of the requirement and will provide additional implementation guidance as necessary. LSC adopts the proposed amendments to § 1630.5 without change.
§ 1630.6 Prior Approval
The existing regulations contain inconsistent language describing the amount of LSC funds that triggers the prior approval requirement. Section 1630.6(b)(1) provides that, without LSC's prior written approval, a recipient may not expend “$25,000 or more” of LSC funds on specified transactions, while § 1631.8(a) applies when a recipient uses “more than $25,000” of LSC funds. The latter formulation reflects the language of the prior version of the rule and the standard LSC intended to apply consistently.
LSC proposed to eliminate this inconsistency and clarify that recipients must obtain prior written approval before incurring a legal obligation to expend LSC funds in excess of the applicable threshold. This clarification reflects LSC's existing enforcement practice and provides recipients with a clearer point at which prior approval is required for procurement planning purposes.
LSC also proposed to increase the prior approval threshold from $25,000 to $50,000. The $25,000 threshold has remained unchanged since 2017 despite inflation, changes in procurement practices, and the increasing complexity of recipient operations. Transactions that may not have warranted individualized review when the threshold was adopted now routinely exceed $25,000. Maintaining the existing threshold may therefore divert recipient and LSC staff resources to transactions that present comparatively lower compliance risks.
LSC Management believes the higher threshold appropriately focuses oversight resources on higher-risk expenditures while reducing an unnecessary administrative burden on recipients. For costs apportioned between LSC funds and one or more other funding sources, prior approval is required when the portion allocable to LSC funds exceeds $50,000.
The final rule also clarifies that recipients must obtain prior approval
before
incurring a legal obligation to expend LSC funds in excess of the applicable threshold. This provision establishes a clear and administrable point at which the approval requirement attaches and avoids uncertainty about whether a recipient may enter a binding agreement before seeking LSC's approval.
Comments:
NLADA supported increasing the prior approval threshold from $25,000 to $50,000 and clarifying that the threshold applies when expenditures exceed $50,000. NLADA stated that the increase would reduce administrative burdens associated with lower-risk transactions and allow recipients and LSC to focus resources on higher-risk expenditures. James Scarborough generally supported increasing the threshold but requested additional explanation for selecting $50,000 and suggested that LSC consider alternatives, including inflation-indexed, grant-specific, or risk-based thresholds. Community Legal Services requested clarification regarding when a recipient “incur[s] a legal obligation to expend LSC funds,” particularly for recurring or month-to-month contracts and costs whose allocation to LSC funds changes over time. He also asked how the standard would address arrangements structured to avoid the prior approval threshold.
Response:
Generally, a recipient must obtain prior approval before incurring a legal obligation to expend more than $50,000 in LSC funds. However, if the recipient cannot reasonably determine the amount it will charge to LSC when it enters into the contract, it must seek prior approval once it reasonably anticipates that its charges to LSC under the contract will exceed $50,000. This may occur, for example, because the recipient requires additional services under a contract or because a change in funding sources increases the portion of the costs allocated to LSC. A recipient that reasonably does not anticipate exceeding the threshold when it enters into the contract does not violate the prior approval requirement by entering into the contract without LSC approval.
For example, a recipient may enter into a multi-year consulting contract without prior approval if, at the outset, it reasonably expects to charge less than $50,000 of the contract costs to LSC funds. If the recipient determines two years into the contract that it will need additional services and realizes that the amount charged to LSC will exceed $50,000, the recipient must seek prior approval at that time. The same principle applies when changes in funding or cost allocations increase the portion of a contract that the recipient expects to charge to LSC funds.
Alternately, if a recipient enters into a multi-year contract under which the amount payable in any single year is less than $50,000, but the recipient knows at the time it enters into the contract that the total amount payable over the term of the contract will exceed $50,000 in LSC funds, then the recipient must obtain prior approval from LSC before entering into the contract.
Recipients remain responsible for monitoring their expenditures and complying with their procurement policies regardless of whether LSC prior approval is initially required. LSC adopts the proposed amendments to § 1630.6 without change.
(
printed page 69723)
B. Part 1631—Purchasing and Property Management
§ 1631.3 Prior Approval Process
Under existing § 1631.3(b), LSC generally must decide whether to approve or deny a request involving purchases or leases of personal property, contracts for services, and capital improvements within 30 days after receiving materials LSC deems sufficient to decide. For purchases of real estate, the corresponding period is 60 days. The regulation also provides that LSC will inform a recipient within 20 days after receiving the initial request whether additional information is necessary.
LSC's experience administering the regulation has demonstrated that complex or atypical requests may require additional information that LSC could not reasonably identify during its initial review. A fixed interpretation of the 30- and 60-day provision could therefore impair LSC's ability to obtain information necessary to evaluate a transaction after the initial review period.
The final rule clarifies how the 30- and 60-day decision periods apply when LSC determines that additional information is necessary to decide a prior approval request. The period runs from LSC's receipt of all materials it deems sufficient to make a decision. If, during its review, LSC determines that more information is necessary, including after LSC has previously requested additional information, the initial, applicable decision period does not continue to run while LSC awaits the requested information. Upon receipt of the additional information, LSC will determine whether the materials are sufficient to make a decision, and the applicable 30- or 60-day decision period will begin from the date LSC has received the materials it deems sufficient. This clarification preserves the existing decision periods while recognizing that LSC may need to request additional information more than once before it has sufficient information to complete its review.
The final rule also increases the threshold applicable to exigent circumstances in § 1631.3(d)(1) from $25,000 to $50,000, consistent with the amendments to §§ 1630.6 and 1631.8.
Comments:
Commenters supported LSC's efforts to clarify and streamline the prior approval process. NLADA specifically supported increasing the prior approval threshold to $50,000 because the higher threshold will reduce administrative burdens associated with lower-risk transactions.
Response:
This amendment maintains consistency with the prior approval threshold established in §§ 1630.6 and 1631.8. LSC adopts the proposed amendments to § 1631.3 without change.
§ 1631.8 Requests for Prior Approval
Consistent with the amendments to § 1630.6, the final rule increases the threshold in § 1631.8(a) from $25,000 to $50,000. A recipient using more than $50,000 of LSC funds to purchase or lease personal property or contract for services must therefore request and receive LSC's prior approval.
LSC also proposed to clarify the documentation required under § 1631.8(b)(3). The existing rule requires documentation showing that the recipient followed its procurement policies and procedures in soliciting, reviewing, and approving the purchase, lease, or contract for services. Recipients have expressed uncertainty about the type of supporting documentation LSC expects, resulting in requests that require supplementation after submission.
The final rule clarifies that the required documentation consists of the documents maintained in the recipient's procurement files that demonstrate adherence to the recipient's procurement policies and procedures. LSC believes this clarification will make the requirement easier to administer and reduce the need for recipients to supplement prior approval requests after submission.
Comments:
Commenters supported increasing the prior approval threshold and aligning the provisions governing when prior approval is required.
Response:
LSC adopts the proposed amendments to § 1631.8 without change.
§ 1631.15 Capital Improvements
Consistent with the amendments to §§ 1630.6, 1631.3, and 1631.8, the final rule increases the threshold in § 1631.15(a) from $25,000 to $50,000. A recipient must obtain LSC's prior written approval before using more than $50,000 LSC funds to make capital improvements to real estate.
Although the NPRM did not specifically identify § 1631.15(a) for revision due to staff omission, the amendment is a logical outgrowth of the proposal pursuant to the Administrative Procedure Act (APA). See
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A)-(B)
. The NPRM expressly proposed increasing the $25,000 threshold to $50,000 in §§§ 1630.6, 1631.3, and 1631.8 under the same circumstances addressed by § 1631.15. The proposal provided sufficient notice, detail, and rationale for LSC's intent to increase the current amount, and does not introduce a new regulatory approach or materially alter the content of the proposal.
Furthermore, a commenter reviewing the proposed amendments to §§§ 1630.3, 1630.6, and 1631.8 reasonably could anticipate that LSC could also make the corresponding change in § 1631.15. Therefore, LSC concludes that the amendment to § 1631.15 is within the scope of the proposed rule and the APA's logical outgrowth doctrine.
Comments:
While commenters did not explicitly review this provision, they supported increasing prior approval thresholds under the same circumstances and aligning provisions governing when prior approval is required.
Response:
LSC adopts the proposed amendments to § 1631.15.
§ 1631.19 Accounting and Reporting to LSC
Existing § 1631.19 requires a recipient to maintain an accounting of LSC funds relating to the purchase or maintenance of real estate purchased with LSC funds and to provide that accounting to LSC no later than April 30 of the following year or in its annual audited financial statements. The April 30 deadline assumes a calendar-year fiscal year and has caused confusion and difficulty for recipients operating on different fiscal calendars.
The final rule eliminates the fixed April 30 deadline. Instead, recipients must provide the required accounting annually no later than the date on which they are required to submit their annual audited financial statements to LSC's Office of Inspector General. Tying the accounting deadline to an existing reporting requirement accommodates recipients with different fiscal years and provides a consistent event-based deadline.
The final rule also clarifies that the accounting is cumulative. A recipient must maintain an accounting of the amount of LSC funds used to pay acquisition, financing, and capital improvement costs for each LSC-funded property, over the life of the property.
In the preamble to the 2016 Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, LSC identified additional costs, including insurance, maintenance, and taxes, as costs for which recipients should account. See
81 FR 75006
,
75017
, Oct. 28, 2016. The regulatory text ultimately required recipients to include only LSC funds used for acquisition costs, financing, and capital improvements. See
82 FR 37327 37344
, Aug. 10, 2017. Since
(
printed page 69724)
promulgating part 1631, LSC has required recipients to report only the categories identified in the regulatory text.
LSC uses this information to determine accurately the amount of LSC funds invested in real property so that, upon disposition, the appropriate amount of proceeds attributable to LSC's investment may be returned to the LSC grant. Insurance and maintenance costs are not included in LSC's assessment of its interest in real estate. Although insurance and maintenance costs allocated to an LSC grant must independently satisfy applicable cost standards, LSC has determined that the administrative cost of including those expenditures in the § 1631.19 accounting exceeds the benefit to LSC.
Comments:
Commenters supported replacing the April 30 deadline with a deadline tied to the submission of individual recipients' annual audited financial statements. James Scarborough recommended that LSC provide implementation guidance or examples regarding the revised accounting deadline, particularly for recipients with different fiscal years and during the transition to the new requirements.
Response:
To address the transition concern raised by James Scarborough, LSC will provide recipients sufficient time and implementation guidance before the revised requirements take effect. Recipients will not be required to resubmit an accounting that became due before the effective date solely to conform to the revised deadline or format. LSC will provide additional implementation guidance as necessary. LSC adopts the proposed amendments to § 1631.9 without change.

AGENCY:
Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is taking final action to approve a revision to the Maricopa County Air Quality Department (MCAQD or “Department”) portion of the Arizona State Implementation Plan (SIP). This revision establishes a federally enforceable program allowing for the generation of emission reduction credits (ERCs) by retrofitting or replacing existing on-road vehicles with lower emitting vehicles while meeting other Clean Air Act (CAA or “Act”) requirements. These ERCs are intended to be used as offsets for major stationary sources under the Department's Nonattainment New Source Review (NNSR) program. The EPA is approving this SIP revision because we find that it meets the applicable CAA requirements.
DATES:
This rule is effective December 7, 2026.

I. Executive Summary
A. What action is the EPA taking?
The EPA is fully approving the Arizona Department of Environmental Quality's (ADEQ's) May 30, 2025, SIP revision for MCAQD Rule 205, “Emission Offsets Generated by Voluntary Mobile Source Emission Reductions,” revised on May 21, 2025 (“Rule 205” or “MCAQD Rule 205 submittal”). Specifically, the EPA is approving the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal by adding Rule 205 into the federally enforceable portion of the Maricopa County portion of the Arizona SIP.
[
1
]
Rule 205 allows for the generation of ERCs through voluntary on-road mobile source emissions reductions. ERCs generated by this rule are intended to be used to offset emissions increases of oxides of nitrogen (NO
X
) and volatile organic compounds (VOC) at major stationary sources as part of the preconstruction permit process required by the CAA's NNSR program.
B. What is the legal authority and what are the requirements?
We are taking this action under CAA section 110. Pursuant to CAA section 110(a), States are required to submit SIPs to the EPA that provide for the implementation, maintenance, and enforcement of the national ambient air quality standards (NAAQS). CAA section 110(k) requires SIPs to meet certain procedural requirements and requires the EPA to approve or disapprove SIP submissions. CAA section 110(l) requires States to provide public notice and an opportunity for public hearing of SIP revisions prior to their submittal and prohibits the EPA from approving any SIP revisions that would interfere with attainment or maintenance of a NAAQS, reasonable further progress, or other CAA applicable requirements. If a SIP submittal meets all the applicable CAA requirements, then the EPA must approve the submittal under CAA section 110(k)(3).
In evaluating the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal, the EPA considered whether ERCs generated under the rule would meet the statutory and regulatory requirements for offsetting emissions reductions in CAA section 173 and
40 CFR 51.165
, respectively. Emissions reductions may generally be credited for NNSR offset purposes under the CAA if they achieve actual emission reductions in the relevant nonattainment area that (1) are not otherwise required by the CAA or relied upon in any air quality-related programs under the CAA; (2) can be reliably quantified using methods that can be replicated; (3) will continue for the duration of the SIP or other program that relies upon the emission reductions; and (4) are enforceable by the EPA under the CAA.
II. Background
The MCAQD is the local air pollution control agency for Maricopa County, Arizona and is responsible for regulating stationary sources of air pollution within its boundaries. Portions of Maricopa County designated nonattainment for the 2008 and 2015 ozone NAAQS are classified as “Moderate” and portions of Maricopa County designated nonattainment for the 1987 particulate matter 10 micrometers or smaller in diameter (PM
10
) NAAQS are classified as “Serious.”
[
2
]
In these nonattainment areas, the MCAQD is required to implement an NNSR permit program for preconstruction review of new or modified major stationary sources.
[
3
]
One of the requirements of the NNSR program is to provide surplus emissions reductions to offset a proposed project's projected emissions increases.
[
4
]
The MCAQD has stated that the quantity of surplus emissions reductions currently available for use as NNSR offsets do not appear sufficient to support current and projected economic growth. To incentivize the generation of additional offsets, the MCAQD developed Rule 205 to create a regulatory structure for the generation and use of NO
X
and VOC ERCs from a nontraditional category. Rule 205 can be used to generate NO
X
and VOC ERCs from on-road mobile sources, or mobile source ERCs (MERCs). The rule allows
(
printed page 69696)
on-road mobile source fleet owners/operators that permanently reduce NO
X
or VOC emissions from their fleets, or credit “generators,” to trade those reductions with stationary sources, or “credit users,” who can then use them to offset their proposed NO
X
or VOC emissions increases for the purpose of meeting NNSR permit requirements.
On April 16, 2026, the EPA proposed approving the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal because we determined that this SIP revision complied with all relevant CAA requirements.
[
5
]

III. Public Comments and EPA Responses
The EPA provided a 30-day public comment period on our proposed action. The comment period opened on April 16, 2026, the date of publication in the
Federal Register
, and closed on May 18, 2026.
[
6
]
During this period, the EPA received comments from five separate commenters. All comments submitted during the public comment period can be found in the docket of this rulemaking.
[
7
]
Four commenters were supportive of the EPA's proposed action.
[
8
]
In addition to support for the proposed action, two of these commenters included additional recommendations for the EPA to consider. One commenter recommended that the EPA: (1) clarify that “future MCAQD revisions incorporating technology-neutral language for software/operational reductions” would be approvable if the offset integrity criteria are satisfied and (2) commit to updating EPA's Economic Incentive Program (EIP) guidance to clarify that “software-driven mobile source reductions can qualify for MERCs/NNSR offsets when properly documented and enforced.” Another commenter encouraged the EPA to continue to take actions that will encourage the generation of ERCs, improve the efficiency of the ERC certification process, and focus on practical actions that could meaningfully improve public health and reduce air pollution. These recommendations from commenters are outside the scope of our final action on the Department's submittal.
One commenter opposed the EPA's proposed action and requested that the EPA disapprove Rule 205. Below, we summarize the commenter's concerns and provide a response to each.
Comment 1:
The commenter asserted that the CAA “does not authorize stationary sources to trade credits with mobile sources because such reductions are not `permanent, quantifiable, and enforceable' as [CAA section] 173(c)(1) requires.” Additionally, the commenter stated Congress separated the authority to regulate stationary sources and mobile sources with no references to linking together with respect to generating offsets.
Response 1:
The EPA disagrees with the commenter's claim that mobile source emissions reductions cannot be used as offsets for stationary sources under CAA section 173(c)(1). CAA section 173(a) conditions the issuance of an NNSR permit on a determination by the permitting agency that, among other things, sufficient offsetting emissions reductions will be obtained before the new or modified source commences operation so as to represent “reasonable further progress” toward attainment of the NAAQS.
[
9
]
The required offsetting emissions reductions must be in effect and enforceable by the time the new or modified source commences operations and must assure that the total tonnage of increased emissions of the relevant air pollutant from the source is offset by an equal or greater reduction, as applicable, in the actual emissions of that air pollutant in the area.
[
10
]
Under CAA section 173(c)(1), ERCs must be obtained from the same source or other sources in the same nonattainment area, except that the reductions may be obtained from another nonattainment area if two conditions are met: (1) the other area has an equal or higher nonattainment classification than the area where the source is located, and (2) emissions from such other area contribute to a violation of the NAAQS in the nonattainment area where the source is located.
[
11
]
These restrictions are designed to ensure that offsets result in the improvement of air quality in the nonattainment area, such that construction (or modification) of the source is consistent with reasonable further progress toward attainment.
[
12
]
Consistent with these statutory requirements, the EPA's NNSR implementing regulations require that all emissions reductions claimed as offset credit be “federally enforceable” and that offsetting emissions reductions be obtained from the same source or other sources in the same nonattainment area, except that the reductions may be obtained from another nonattainment area if the two conditions specified in CAA section 173(c)(1) are met.
[
13
]
Additionally, the EPA's NNSR regulations provide that emissions reductions achieved by shutting down an existing emission unit or curtailing production or operating hours may be credited for offsets only if, among other things, the reductions are surplus, permanent, quantifiable, and federally
(
printed page 69697)
enforceable.
[
14
]
The EPA has referred to these four creditability criteria in longstanding guidance as “integrity elements”—
i.e.,
elements of a program that ensure it has integrity and meets applicable statutory requirements.
[
15
]
The EPA sometimes refers to these integrity elements, along with the requirement in CAA section 173(c)(1) that offsets be based on the reduction of “actual” emissions of the relevant pollutant, as the offset “integrity criteria.”
[
16
]
To the extent the commenter intended to assert that stationary sources are regulated under title I of the CAA while mobile sources are regulated under title II of the CAA, this is generally correct. But nothing in CAA section 173 or any other provision of the CAA prohibits the use of emissions reductions from mobile sources within the relevant nonattainment area for NNSR offset purposes, provided the applicable statutory and regulatory requirements are met. The commenter fails to identify any such prohibition in the text of the CAA or the EPA's implementing regulations. The commenter also fails to support its claim that mobile source emissions reductions would not meet the permanent, quantifiable, and federally enforceable offset integrity criteria.
[
17
]
The EPA's proposed rule and TSD explained in detail how Rule 205 meets the applicable CAA requirements and addresses the EPA's longstanding integrity criteria for offsetting emissions reductions. In the next few paragraphs, we briefly summarize our prior analysis of the permanent, quantifiable, and federally enforceable criteria.
To ensure emissions reductions from mobile sources meet the permanent criterion, generators of MERCs must demonstrate that replaced vehicles no longer operate in the nonattainment area (NAA) and/or that emissions do not shift to higher emitting vehicles within the fleet. Generators of MERCs do so through enforceable requirements, including robust monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. Rule 205 contains several enforceable conditions to ensure that emissions reductions are permanent, including: limiting the applicability of the rule to “captive fleet”
[
18
]
vehicles; requiring the original baseline vehicle to be permanently removed from the Maricopa NAA or rendered permanently disabled and disposed of;
[
19
]
requiring any future replacement of the new or retrofitted fleet vehicle to be with a vehicle that is certified to the same or lower emission standard;
[
20
]
and related monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements.
[
21 22
]
To ensure emissions reductions from mobile sources meet the quantifiable criterion, generators of MERCs calculate emissions reductions using specific methodologies that are clear and replicable. Appendix A of Rule 205 articulates the calculation formula that MERC generators will use to determine the number of eligible MERCs.
[
23
]
Rule 205 requires MERC generators to submit information, within their MERC application, on the methodology for quantifying emissions reductions, including emissions calculations and documentation of each original vehicle's historic vehicle miles traveled.
[
24 25
]
Rule 205 also requires MERC generators to demonstrate that the captive fleet of vehicles used to generate MERCs are based and operated within the NAA.
[
26
]
Finally, Rule 205 requires the MCAQD to evaluate whether the proposed qualifying emission reductions within the application for MERCs will result in quantifiable emission reductions.
[
27 28
]
To meet the requirement in
40 CFR 51.165(a)(3)(ii)(E)
that offsetting emissions reductions be federally enforceable, emissions reductions must be enforceable by the EPA and must be legally and practicably enforceable. The term “federally enforceable” is defined in the EPA's regulations at
40 CFR 51.165(a)(1)(xiv)
to mean “all limitations and conditions which are enforceable by the Administrator,” including those requirements developed pursuant to
40 CFR parts 60
and
61
, requirements within any applicable SIP, and any permit requirements established pursuant to
40 CFR 52.21
or under regulations approved pursuant to
40 CFR part 51, subpart I
. Additionally, reductions are legally and practicably enforceable if the reductions can be independently verified; violations of the program that generated the credits are defined and those liable for the violations can be identified; access to the emissions-related information underlying the credits is available; and the public can file civil lawsuits to enforce violations.
[
29
]
The EPA's approval of Rule 205 into the SIP ensures that MERCs issued under the rule are federally enforceable. In addition, after determining that the requested reductions meet the certification criteria, the permits that MCAQD issues pursuant to its SIP-approved NNSR program incorporate requirements that make the reductions in qualifying emissions federally enforceable.
[
30 31
]
Based on our evaluation, we find that Rule 205 ensures that offsetting emissions reductions will be permanent, quantifiable, and federally enforceable consistent with the requirements of CAA section 173 and
40 CFR 51.165
.
Comment 2:
The commenter stated that Rule 205 measures emissions reductions solely at the tailpipe, relies on the EPA's MOtor Vehicle Emission Simulator (MOVES) based emission factors, and excludes “upstream NO
X
and VOC emissions associated with electricity generation and transmission needed to power replacement battery electric vehicles.” Therefore, the commenter believes these actions can, in effect, overstate actual emissions reductions. Because CAA section 173(c)(1) requires emissions increases to be offset by the “actual emissions” of such air pollutant within the nonattainment area, the commenter requested the EPA account for upstream
(
printed page 69698)
“lifecycle” emissions increases associated with charging electric vehicles by “requiring MCAQD to include, at minimum, a qualitative disclosure in each MERC application identifying the electricity source and associated upstream NO
X
and VOC emissions.”
Response 2:
The EPA disagrees with the claim that to approve Rule 205 the EPA must account for upstream “lifecycle” emissions potentially associated with charging electric vehicles by requiring the MCAQD to include a qualitative disclosure in each MERC application identifying the electricity source and upstream NO
X
and VOC emissions. As an initial matter, we note that Rule 205 is designed to be broadly applicable, and MERCs can be generated using any fuel type (
e.g.,
replacing a diesel engine with a lower-emitting diesel engine). That is, Rule 205 is fuel neutral and not every MERC application will be for electric vehicles, as suggested by the comment.
The commenter's concern that the use of MOVES can overstate the actual emissions reductions eligible for offsets when a vehicle is replaced with an electric vehicle raises a hypothetical, fact-specific issue that is best evaluated in the context of an individual MERC application. The commenter specifically cited to the requirement in CAA section 173(c)(1) that requires emissions increases to “be offset by an equal or greater reduction, as applicable, in the actual emissions of such air pollutant from the same or other sources in the area.” As we explained in our proposal, this means the emissions reductions must be “real” and not a theoretical reduction in the source's potential to emit; in other words, it requires that each offset represents emissions that have been taken out of the air.
[
32
]
The requirements of Rule 205 ensure that this requirement will be met. For example, before granting MERCs, Rule 205 requires the MCAQD to evaluate whether the emissions reductions will be real and include an opportunity for public comment on the Department's evaluation.
[
33
]
The rule also defines “real” as “[a] reduction in actual emissions previously released into the air resulting from a physical change or change to the method of operation by a generator.”
[
34
]
Thus, no revisions to Rule 205 are needed to ensure CAA section 173(c)(1) will be met. While the MERC calculation methodology in Appendix A of Rule 205 is meant to be applicable to most situations, if the MCAQD determines that not all of the emissions reductions for a specific project would be real, then the MERC generator could potentially obtain approval from the MCAQD and the EPA for an alternative MERC calculation method.
[
35
]
Regardless of the calculation method used, the Department must determine that the requested MERCs will result in real, quantifiable, federally enforceable, permanent, and surplus emissions reductions prior to the MERC generator requesting a permit or permit revision to impose conditions to make the emissions reductions permanent and enforceable.
[
36
]
Comment 3:
The commenter stated that Appendix A of Rule 205, which contains the equation used to quantify the number of MERCs, and the MCAQD's EIP support document effectively only addresses electric vehicles. The MOVES model does not “separately represent hybrid, plug-in hybrid, CNG [compressed natural gas], LNG [liquefied natural gas], or other alternative-fuel vehicles as distinct source types” and, as a result, non-electric vehicle projects may rely on default MOVES assumptions that do not reflect actual emissions and undermine the “quantifiability and integrity of generated MERCs.”
Response 3:
The EPA disagrees with the commenter's claim that the quantification method in Rule 205 can only be used to generate MERCs through replacing vehicles with electric vehicles. In 2025, MCAQD revised the quantification method in Rule 205 to ensure the rule is fuel neutral. Owners/operators of vehicle fleets can opt to choose any available vehicle type as a replacement as long as it would emit less NO
X
and VOC, including diesel, compressed natural gas, gasoline/diesel hybrids, plug-in hybrids, and electric vehicles.
The emission rates within MOVES differ by the vehicle type and by the fuel type used, as well as other aspects of vehicles and their activity.
[
37 38
]
Rule 205 identifies fuel type as one of the data points required to run MOVES.
[
39
]
Therefore, the necessary inputs to quantify MERCs are well defined in Rule 205, ensuring emissions from all fuel types are quantifiable under Rule 205.
[
40 41
]
Comment 4:
The commenter stated that the surplus requirement mandates that credited reductions must not otherwise be required by the CAA and, therefore, MERCs must account for tightening Federal vehicle standards. The commenter stated that as EPA emissions standards progressively reduce NO
X
and non-methane organic gas emissions, “the emissions factors embedded in MOVES will increasingly reflect reductions mandated by [F]ederal law,” which would not qualify as voluntary or surplus reductions. Essentially, “[r]ule 205 addresses surplus only at the point of application and fails to ensure that credits remain `surplus' as [F]ederal vehicle standards tighten.”
Response 4:
We disagree with the commenter's claim that Rule 205 fails to ensure that MERCs remain surplus as Federal vehicle standards tighten. While not specifically stated in the comment, we assume the commenter is referring to the concept of “fleet turnover,” where the totality of the vehicles in an area will emit less air pollutants over time because of the natural cycle of vehicle owners replacing their vehicles with newer models, which are typically subject to more stringent vehicle emissions standards. Because CAA section 173(c)(2) expressly states that “[e]mission reductions otherwise required by [the CAA] shall not be creditable as emissions reductions for purposes of any such offset requirement,” emissions reductions used to demonstrate attainment of the NAAQS or to meet transportation conformity requirements would not be creditable for NNSR offset purposes under CAA section 173.
To ensure MERCs are surplus and meet the requirements of CAA section 173(c)(2), the MCAQD Rule 205
(
printed page 69699)
submittal explains that the Maricopa Association of Governments (MAG)
[
42
]
will address this by adding 1,000 tpy of NO
X
and 500 tpy of VOC emissions into the emissions inventory for its new ozone “Moderate” area plan for the 2015 ozone NAAQS.
[
43
]
This line item represents the maximum number of MERCs and/or nonroad engine emission reduction credits (NERCs) that will be creditable through Rule 205 and MCAQD Rule 204, “Emission Offsets Generated by Voluntary Nonroad Engine Emission Reductions,” revised on November 5, 2025 (“Rule 204”).
[
44
]
Effectively, this ensures MERCs and NERCs generated through Rules 205 and 204, respectively, will be excluded from SIP modeling and cannot be accounted for in the State's attainment demonstration for the 2015 ozone NAAQS. Regarding transportation conformity, the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal explains that before the start of modeling for a transportation plan or transportation improvement program conformity, the MCAQD will notify MAG of each individual MERC project so that the reductions from each project are not included in the corresponding transportation conformity analysis, consistent with the interagency consultation process required by
40 CFR 93.112
.
[
45
]
These actions by the MCAQD and MAG related to attainment plans and transportation conformity ensure that Rule 205 will only allow surplus emissions reductions to be creditable for NNSR offset purposes and that Arizona will not “double-count” emissions reductions when developing SIP attainment demonstrations.
Comment 5.a:
The commenter asserted that Rule 205 is deficient because it does not specify whether ongoing monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements applicable to MERC generators must be preserved when the generator's business changes hands, restructures, expands, or shuts down. The commenter asserted that this omission is a legal defect.
Response 5.a:
We disagree that Rule 205 is deficient because it does not specifically state what happens to ongoing requirements in Rule 205 when the MERC generator's business changes hands, restructures, expands, or shuts down. Under Rule 205, MERC generators will be issued permits that contain the applicable monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements.
[
46
]
If the owner/operator named on the permit were to change as a result of a business changing hands, restructuring, expanding, or shutting down, the MCAQD's SIP-approved New Source Review (NSR) program provides a process for ensuring that permit requirements remain in effect, and this process would apply to MERC generators.
[
47
]
MCAQD Rule 200, “Permit Requirements,” revised on December 11, 2019 (“Rule 200”), describes the requirements for transferring a permit, including, but not limited to, a signed statement and acceptance of responsibility for the permit by the new permit holder.
[
48
]
To the extent the commenter is concerned about the integrity of MERCs as a result of a business changing hands, restructuring, expanding, or shutting down, Rule 205 contains provisions for ensuring the ongoing integrity of MERCs and includes requirements to address potential shortfalls in emissions reductions.
[
49
]
Comment 5.b:
The commenter stated that the requirement for MERC generators in Rule 205 to track, for 20 years, that a new or retrofitted vehicle is only replaced with a vehicle that is certified to the same or lower emission standards is a “de facto constraint on future fleet decisions.” As an example, the commenter stated that a company that switches to electric vehicles but leases vehicles on a three-year cycle could be prohibited from reverting to internal combustion engines at the end of the lease term, which the commenter asserted would effectively function as a long-term electric vehicle mandate. The commenter concluded that the rule therefore “raises significant preemption concerns absent a [CAA] [s]ection 209 waiver.”
Response 5.b:
We disagree that Rule 205 functions as a long-term electric vehicle mandate that raises preemption concerns under CAA section 209. CAA section 209(a) prohibits States from setting or enforcing new motor vehicle emissions standards unless a waiver is granted by the EPA under CAA section 209(b).
[
50
]
Here, there is no State action to set or enforce a new motor vehicle emissions standard. Rule 205 is merely an administrative rule to facilitate the creation and trading of MERCs for use as offsets by stationary sources. Participation in the MERC generating program is voluntary. If a fleet owner or operator voluntarily
chooses
to generate MERCs by replacing a vehicle with an electric vehicle, then Rule 205 requires the MERC generator to maintain the same level of emissions reductions for 20 years to meet the offset integrity criteria. As stated previously, Rule 205 is fuel neutral and does not restrict the type of vehicle replacement that qualifies for generating MERCs. If a MERC generator finds that replacing a vehicle with an electric vehicle would be too restrictive on future vehicle fleet decisions, then the MERC generator can choose a replacement vehicle type with emission rates the MERC generator can more confidently maintain.
IV. EPA Action
No comments were submitted that changed our assessment of the approvability of the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal as described in our proposed action. Therefore, as authorized in CAA section 110(k)(3), the EPA is approving the MCAQD Rule 205 submittal by adding MCAQD Rule 205 into the federally enforceable portion of the Arizona SIP and adding the MCAQD's EIP support document into the non-regulatory portion of the Arizona SIP.

In this document, the EPA is finalizing regulatory text that includes incorporation by reference. In accordance with requirements of
1 CFR 51.5

(

Department of Education
AGENCY:
U.S. Department of Education, Office of Postsecondary Education.
ACTION:
Call for written third-party comments.
SUMMARY:
This notice provides information to members of the public on submitting written comments for accrediting agencies currently undergoing review for the purpose of recognition by the Secretary of Education.
DATES:
Comments must be received on or before 30 days from publication of this notice in the
Federal Register
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Elizabeth Daggett, Director, Accreditation Group, Office of Postsecondary Education, U.S. Department of Education, 400 Maryland Ave. SW, Washington, DC 20202, telephone: (202) 453-7615, or email:
elizabeth.daggett@ed.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This request for written third-party comments concerning the performance of accrediting agencies under review by the Secretary of Education is required by Section 496(n)(1)(A) of the Higher Education Act of 1965, as amended,
20 U.S.C. 1001
,
et seq.
(HEA), and pertains to the third meeting in 2027 of the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI). The meeting date will be announced in a later
Federal Register
notice and will describe how to register to provide oral comments at the meeting. Written comments submitted in response to this
Federal Register
notice must be submitted to the electronic mail address identified below on or before the comment due date.
Agencies Under Review and Evaluation:
The Department requests written comments from the public on the following accrediting agencies, which are currently undergoing review and evaluation by the Accreditation Group, and which will be reviewed at the third 2027 NACIQI meeting.
The agencies are listed by the type of application each agency has submitted. Please note, each agency's current scope of recognition is indicated below. If any agency requested to expand its scope of recognition, both the current scope of recognition and the requested scope of recognition are identified below.
Applications for Renewal of Recognition
1. Accrediting Commission for Education in Nursing, Inc. Scope of Recognition: The accreditation of nursing education programs and schools, both postsecondary and higher degree, which offer a certificate, diploma, or a recognized professional degree including clinical doctorate, master's, baccalaureate, associate, diploma, and practical nursing programs including those offered via distance education. Geographic Area of Accrediting Activities: Throughout the United States.
2. Accreditation Commission for Midwifery Education. Scope of Recognition: The accreditation and preaccreditation of basic certificate, basic graduate nurse-midwifery, direct entry midwifery, and pre-certification nurse-midwifery education programs, including those programs that offer distance education. Geographic Area of Accrediting Activities: Throughout the United States.
3. American Physical Therapy Association, Commission on Accreditation in Physical Therapy Education. Scope of Recognition: The accreditation and preaccreditation (“Candidate for Accreditation”) of physical therapist education programs leading to the first professional degree at the master's or doctoral level and physical therapist assistant education programs at the associate degree level and for its accreditation of such programs offered via distance education. Geographic Area of Accrediting Activities: Throughout the United States.
4. Higher Learning Commission. Scope of Recognition: The accreditation and preaccreditation (“Candidate for Accreditation”) of degree-granting institutions, including tribal institutions, and the accreditation of programs offered via distance education, correspondence courses, and direct assessment within these institutions. This recognition extends to the Institutional Actions Council jointly with the Board of Trustees of the Commission for decisions on cases for continued accreditation or reaffirmation, and continued candidacy, and to the Appeals Body jointly with the Board of Trustees of the Commission for decisions related to initial candidacy or accreditation or reaffirmation of accreditation. Geographic Area of
(
printed page 69827)
Accrediting Activities: Throughout the United States.
5. Middle States Commission on Higher Education. Scope of Recognition: The accreditation and preaccreditation (“Candidacy status”) of institutions of higher education including distance, correspondence education programs and direct assessment programs offered at those institutions. Recognition extends to the Executive Committee to act on behalf of the Commission as necessary on cases of initial, reaffirmed, and continued candidacy or initial, reaffirmed and continued accreditation. Geographic Area of Accrediting Activities: Throughout the United States.
6. New England Commission of Higher Education. Scope of recognition: The accreditation and preaccreditation (“Candidacy status”) of institutions of higher education including the accreditation of programs offered via distance education and direct assessment within those institutions. Jointly with the Commission, this recognition extends to its Executive Committee and also to the Appeals Body for decisions related to the appeal of denial or withdrawal of candidacy; probation; and denial or withdrawal of accreditation. Geographic Area of Accrediting Activities: Throughout the United States.
7. New York State Board of Regents (Public Postsecondary Vocational Education, Practical Nursing). Scope of Recognition: State agency for the approval of public postsecondary vocational education in the field of practical nursing, including via distance education, offered by a Board of Cooperative Educational Services, an Educational Opportunity Center, City School Districts, and County Boards of Supervisors to prepare persons for licensed practical nursing careers in the State of New York.
8. Oklahoma Department of Career and Technology Education. Scope of Recognition: State agency for the approval of public postsecondary vocational education.
9. Pennsylvania State Board of Career and Technical Education. Scope of Recognition: State agency for the approval of public postsecondary vocational education.
10. WASC Senior College and University Commission. Scope of recognition: The accreditation and preaccreditation (“Candidate for Accreditation”) of institutions of higher education that offer the baccalaureate degree or above, including distance education programs offered at those institutions. Geographic Area of Accrediting Activities: Throughout the United States.
Requested scope of recognition:
The accreditation and preaccreditation (“Candidate for Accreditation”) of institutions of higher education, including programs offered by those institutions via distance education and/or using direct assessment. This recognition extends to the Executive Committee. Geographic Area of Accrediting Activities: Throughout the United States.
Submission of Written Comments Regarding a Specific Accrediting Agency or State Agency Under Review
Written comments in response to this
Federal Register
notice about the recognition of any of the accrediting agencies listed above must be received on or before the comment due date, in the
ThirdPartyComments@ed.gov
mailbox. Please include in the subject line “Written Comments: (agency name).” The electronic mail (email) must include the name(s), title, organization/affiliation, mailing address, email address, and telephone number of the person(s) making the comment. Comments should be submitted as a PDF, Microsoft Word document, or in a medium compatible with Microsoft Word that is attached to an email or provided in the body of an email message. Comments about an agency that has submitted a petition for initial recognition, renewal of recognition, or an expansion of scope must relate to the agency's compliance with the Criteria for the recognition of Accrediting Agencies, which are available at:
https://www.ecfr.gov/​current/​title-34/​subtitle-B/​chapter-VI/​part-602?​toc=​1
.
Only written materials submitted by the deadline to the email address listed in this notice, and in accordance with these instructions, become part of the official record concerning agencies scheduled for review and are considered by the Department and NACIQI in their deliberations. Comments about the agencies listed in this
Federal Register
notice may also be provided orally at the third 2027 NACIQI meeting, which has not yet been scheduled, but which will be announced in a future
Federal Register
notice.
