Appendix
Scope of the Order
The merchandise covered by the
Order
is aluminum common alloy sheet (common alloy sheet), which is a flat-rolled aluminum product having a thickness of 6.3 mm or less, but greater than 0.2 mm, in coils or cut-to-length, regardless of width. Common alloy sheet within the scope of the
Order
includes both not clad aluminum sheet, as well as multi-alloy, clad aluminum sheet. With respect to not clad aluminum sheet, common alloy sheet is manufactured from a 1XXX-, 3XXX-, or 5XXX-series alloy as designated by the Aluminum Association. With respect to multi-alloy, clad aluminum sheet, common alloy sheet is produced from a 3XXX-series core, to which cladding layers are applied to either one or both sides of the core.
Common alloy sheet may be made to ASTM specification B209-14, but can also be made to other specifications. Regardless of specification, however, all common alloy sheet meeting the scope description is included in the scope. Subject merchandise includes common alloy sheet that has been further processed in a third country, including but not limited to annealing, tempering, painting, varnishing, trimming, cutting, punching, and/or slitting, or any other processing that would not otherwise remove the merchandise from the scope of the
Order
if performed in the country of manufacture of the common alloy sheet.
Excluded from the scope of these
Order
is aluminum can stock, which is suitable for use in the manufacture of aluminum beverage cans, lids of such cans, or tabs used to open such cans. Aluminum can stock is produced to gauges that range from 0.200 mm to 0.292 mm, and has an H-19, H-41, H-48, H-39, or H-391 temper. In addition, aluminum can stock has a lubricant applied to the flat surfaces of the can stock to facilitate its movement through machines used in the manufacture of beverage cans. Aluminum can stock is generally classifiable under Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the United States (HTSUS) subheadings 7606.12.3045 and 7606.12.3055; however, the written description of aluminum can stock covered by the scope exclusion set forth above is dispositive, regardless of HTSUS classification.
Where the nominal and actual measurements vary, a product is within the scope if application of either the nominal or actual measurement would place it within the scope based on the definitions set for the above.
Common alloy sheet is currently classifiable under HTSUS subheadings 7606.11.3060, 7606.11.6000, 7606.12.3090, 7606.12.6000, 7606.91.3090, 7606.91.6080, 7606.92.3090, and 7606.92.6080. Further, merchandise that falls within the scope of the
Order
may also be entered into the United States under HTSUS subheadings 7606.11.3030, 7606.12.3030, 7606.91.3060, 7606.91.6040, 7606.92.3060, 7606.92.6040, 7607.11.9090. Although the HTSUS subheadings are provided for convenience and customs purposes, the written description of the scope of the
Order
is dispositive.

ad valorem

ad valorem
or per-unit rate is greater than

(

ad valorem

Notice is hereby given pursuant to the Antitrust Procedures and Penalties Act,
15 U.S.C. 16(b)-(h)
, that the Amended Response of Plaintiff United States to Public Comments on the Proposed Final Judgment has been filed with the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio, Eastern Division in
United States of America, et al.
v.
OhioHealth Corporation,
Civil Action No. 2:26-cv-207.
Copies of the Public Comments and the United States' Amended Response are available for inspection on the Antitrust Division's website at
http://www.justice.gov/​atr
and at the Office of the Clerk of the United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio. Copies of these materials may be obtained from the Antitrust Division upon request and payment of the copying fee set by Department of Justice regulations.
Suzanne Morris,
Deputy Director of Civil Enforcement Operations, Antitrust Division.
United States District Court for the Southern District of Ohio Eastern Division
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA and STATE OF OHIO, Plaintiffs, v. OHIOHEALTH CORPORATION, Defendant.
Case No. 2:26-cv-207
Judge Algenon L. Marbley
Magistrate Judge S. Courter M. Shimeall
Amended Response of Plaintiff United States to Public Comments on the Proposed Final Judgment
Pursuant to the Antitrust Procedures and Penalties Act,
15 U.S.C. 16(b)-(h)
(the “Tunney Act” or “APPA”), the United States submits this amended response to the public comments it received regarding the proposed Final Judgment in this case. The United States received four comments about the proposed remedy, which are summarized and addressed below and attached as Exhibit A. This is an amended response to the United States' Response to Public Comments on the Proposed Final Judgment (“Response to Comments”), filed on October 20, 2026. (Dkt. 34). The United States has amended its response to address a comment that had been inadvertently omitted from its initial response. Other than this paragraph, references to the number of comments received, and the addition of the comment to Exhibit A, the only changes from the initial Response to Comments are on pages 12-13. After careful consideration of the submitted comments, the United States continues to believe that the proposed Final Judgment is in the public interest because it will provide an effective and appropriate remedy for the antitrust violations the Complaint alleged.
Specifically, the proposed Final Judgment will protect competition by, among other things, voiding the anticompetitive steering and transparency restrictions, prohibiting OhioHealth Corporation (“OhioHealth”) from seeking or obtaining such provisions in the future, and prohibiting OhioHealth from penalizing payors that engage (or are planning to engage) in steering, offer steered plans, or provide price transparency to their members.
After this response has been published in the
Federal Register
, pursuant to
15 U.S.C. 16(d)
, the United States will move that the Court enter the proposed Final Judgment.
(
printed page 69866)
I. Procedural History
On February 20, 2026, the United States, along with the State of Ohio, filed a civil antitrust Complaint (Dkt. 1) seeking to enjoin OhioHealth's alleged anticompetitive steering and transparency restrictions. The Complaint alleges that OhioHealth engaged in anticompetitive contracting that reduced choice for consumers and prevented price competition for healthcare services in the Columbus area in violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act,
15 U.S.C. 1
.
On June 16, 2026, Plaintiffs filed the proposed Final Judgment, as well as a stipulation signed by all parties consenting to entry of the proposed Final Judgment after compliance with the requirements of the Tunney Act. (Dkt. 29-1, 29-2). On July 15, 2026, the United States filed a Competitive Impact Statement describing the proposed Final Judgment. (Dkt. 33).
The United States arranged for the publication of the Complaint, the proposed Final Judgment, and the Competitive Impact Statement in the
Federal Register
on July 23, 2026 (
see
91 FR 46463
(2026)), and caused notice regarding the same, together with directions for the submission of written comments relating to the proposed Final Judgment, to be published in the
Washington Post
and
The Columbus Dispatch
from July 27, 2026, through August 3, 2026. The four public comments received in response are described below and attached as Exhibit A. The 60-day period for public comment has now ended.
II. Standard of Judicial Review
Under the Tunney Act, proposed Final Judgments, or “consent judgments,” in antitrust cases brought by the United States are subject to a 60-day comment period, after which the Court shall determine whether entry of the proposed Final Judgment “is in the public interest.”
15 U.S.C. 16(e)(1)
. In making that determination, the Tunney Act, as amended in 2004, directs the Court to consider the following factors:
(a) the competitive impact of such judgment, including termination of alleged violations, provisions for enforcement and modification, duration of relief sought, anticipated effects of alternative remedies actually considered, whether its terms are ambiguous, and any other competitive considerations bearing upon the adequacy of such judgment that the court deems necessary to a determination of whether the consent judgment is in the public interest; and
(b) the impact of entry of such judgment upon competition in the relevant market or markets, upon the public generally and individuals alleging specific injury from the violations set forth in the complaint including consideration of the public benefit, if any, to be derived from a determination of the issues at trial.
15 U.S.C. 16(e)(1)(A)
& (B).
In considering these statutory factors, the Court's inquiry is necessarily a limited one, as the government is entitled to “broad discretion to settle with the defendant within the reaches of the public interest.”
United States
v.
Microsoft Corp.,
56 F.3d 1448, 1461 (D.C. Cir. 1995);
United States
v.
Hewlett Packard Enter. Co.,
No. 25-CV-00951-PCP, 2026 WL 2349970, at *16 (N.D. Cal. Aug. 12, 2026);
United States
v.
U.S. Airways Grp., Inc.,
38 F. Supp. 3d 69, 75 (D.D.C. 2014) (explaining that the “court's inquiry is limited” in Tunney Act settlements);
United States
v.
InBev N.V./S.A.,
No. 08-1965 (JR), 2009 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 84787, at *3 (D.D.C. Aug. 11, 2009) (noting that a court's review of a proposed final judgment is limited and only inquires “into whether the government's determination that the proposed remedies will cure the antitrust violations alleged in the complaint [is] reasonable, and whether the mechanisms to enforce the final judgment are clear and manageable”);
United States
v.
Charleston Area Med. Ctr., Inc.,
No. 2:16-3664, 2016 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 145963 at *5 (S.D.W.V. Oct. 21, 2016) (“In evaluating whether the proposed final judgment is in the public interest, the inquiry is `a narrow one.' ” (quoting
Massachusetts
v.
Microsoft Corp.,
372 F.3d 1199, 1236 (D.C. Cir. 2004))).
Under the Tunney Act, a court considers, among other things, the relationship between the remedy secured and the specific allegations in the government's complaint, whether the proposed final judgment is sufficiently clear, whether its enforcement mechanisms are sufficient, and whether it may positively harm third parties.
See Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1458-62. With respect to the adequacy of the relief secured by the proposed Final Judgment, a court may not “make de novo determination of facts and issues.”
United States
v.
W. Elec. Co.,
993 F.2d 1572, 1577 (D.C. Cir. 1993) (quotation marks omitted);
see also Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1460-62;
United States
v.
Alcoa, Inc.,
152 F. Supp. 2d 37, 40 (D.D.C. 2001);
United States
v.
Enova Corp.,
107 F. Supp. 2d 10, 16 (D.D.C. 2000);
InBev,
2009 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 84787, at *3. Instead, “[t]he balancing of competing social and political interests affected by a proposed antitrust [judgment] must be left, in the first instance, to the discretion of the Attorney General.”
W. Elec. Co.,
993 F.2d at 1577 (quotation marks omitted). “The court should also bear in mind the
flexibility
of the public interest inquiry: the court's function is not to determine whether the resulting array of rights and liabilities is the one that will
best
serve society, but only to confirm that the resulting settlement is within the
reaches
of the public interest.”
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1460 (internal quotation marks omitted) (emphasis in original);
see also United States
v.
Deutsche Telekom AG,
No. 19-2232 (TJK), 2020 WL 1873555, at *7 (D.D.C. Apr. 14, 2020). More demanding requirements would “have enormous practical consequences for the government's ability to negotiate future settlements,” contrary to congressional intent.
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1456. “The Tunney Act was not intended to create a disincentive to the use of the consent [judgment].”
Id.
“Because enforcement by consent decree is an alternative to enforcement by trial or abandonment of the litigation altogether and often reflects the United States's assessment of litigation risk, a proposed settlement does not need to replicate the full relief that [the] United States sought in its complaint.”
Hewlett Packard Enter.,
2026 WL 2349970, at *17. The United States' predictions about the efficacy of the remedy are to be afforded deference by the Court.
See, e.g., Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1461 (recognizing courts should give “due respect to the Justice Department's . . . view of the nature of its case”);
United States
v.
Republic Servs., Inc.,
723 F. Supp. 2d 157, 160 (D.D.C. 2010) (noting “the deferential review to which the government's proposed remedy is accorded”);
United States
v.
Archer-Daniels-Midland Co.,
272 F. Supp. 2d 1, 6 (D.D.C. 2003) (“A district court must accord due respect to the government's prediction as to the effect of proposed remedies, its perception of the market structure, and its view of the nature of the case.”). The ultimate question is whether “the remedies [obtained by the Final Judgment are] so inconsonant with the allegations charged as to fall outside of the `reaches of the public interest.' ”
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1461.
Moreover, the Court's role under the Tunney Act is limited to reviewing the remedy in relationship to the violations that the United States has alleged in its Complaint and does not authorize the Court to “construct [its] own hypothetical case and then evaluate the decree against that case.”
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1459;
see also U.S. Airways,
38
(
printed page 69867)
F. Supp. 3d at 75 (noting that the court must simply determine whether there is a factual foundation for the government's decisions such that its conclusions regarding the proposed settlements are reasonable);
InBev,
2009 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 84787, at *20 (“[T]he `public interest' is not to be measured by comparing the violations alleged in the complaint against those the court believes could have, or even should have, been alleged.”). Because the “court's authority to review the decree depends entirely on the government's exercising its prosecutorial discretion by bringing a case in the first place,” it follows that “the court is only authorized to review the decree itself,” and not to “effectively redraft the complaint” to inquire into other matters that the United States did not pursue.
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1459-60;
see also United States
v.
Alcan Aluminium, Ltd.,
605 F. Supp. 619, 622 (W.D. Ky. 1985) (approving the consent decree even though the court would have imposed a greater remedy).
Further, “[i]n evaluating objections to settlement agreements under the Tunney Act, a court must be mindful that [t]he government need not prove that the settlements will perfectly remedy the alleged antitrust harms[;] it need only provide a factual basis for concluding that the settlements are reasonably adequate remedies for the alleged harms.”
United States
v.
Iron Mountain, Inc.,
217 F. Supp. 3d 146, 152-53 (D.D.C. 2016) (second and third alterations in original) (internal citations omitted). The Court's authority is essentially binary: it may approve a proposed final judgment that falls within the “reaches of the public interest,” or it may reject one that does not.
Microsoft,
56 F.3d at 1461-62. “Short of that eventuality, the Tunney Act cannot be interpreted as an authorization for a district judge to assume the role of Attorney General.”
Id.
at 1462.
[
1
]
In its 2004 amendments to the Tunney Act, Congress made clear its intent to preserve the practical benefits of using judgments proposed by the United States in antitrust enforcement and added the unambiguous instruction that “[n]othing in this section shall be construed to require the court to conduct an evidentiary hearing or to require the court to permit anyone to intervene.”
Public Law 108-237
,  221, 118 Stat. 668-69 (codified as amended at
15 U.S.C. 16(e)(2)
). This Court itself has held that the 2004 amendments to the APPA “do not enlarge the scope of the court's public interest review.”
United States
v.
Fed'n of Physicians & Dentists,
No. 1:05-cv-431, 2008 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 133904, at *5-6, *6 n.1 (S.D. Ohio Apr. 22, 2008) (citing
United States
v.
SBC Commc'ns Inc.,
489 F. Supp. 2d 1, 15 (D.D.C. 2007) (“[T]he Court cannot look beyond the complaint in making the public interest determination unless the complaint is drafted so narrowly as to make a mockery of judicial power.”)). As Senator Tunney explained: “The court is nowhere compelled to go to trial or to engage in extended proceedings which might have the effect of vitiating the benefits of prompt and less costly settlement through the consent [judgment] process.” 119 Cong. Rec. 24,598 (1973) (statement of Sen. Tunney). “A court can make its public interest determination based on the competitive impact statement and response to public comments alone.”
U.S. Airways,
38 F. Supp. 3d at 76 (citing
Enova Corp.,
107 F. Supp. 2d at 17).
III. The Harm Alleged in the Complaint and the Proposed Final Judgment
The proposed Final Judgment resolves the United States' claim that OhioHealth has maintained provisions in its contracts with payors that (1) prevent payors from steering away from OhioHealth to incentivize patients to use less-expensive providers than OhioHealth and (2) inhibit payors from informing patients that less-expensive options are available. As alleged in the Complaint, these restrictions deprive Columbus-area consumers of the choice of lower-cost health plan options and reduce competition among hospitals in violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act,
15 U.S.C. 1
(“Sherman Act claim”).
OhioHealth is a not-for-profit healthcare services corporation, with its principal place of business in Columbus, Ohio. OhioHealth owns or manages sixteen hospitals and outpatient facilities, physician groups, and other healthcare services throughout Ohio.
As alleged in the Complaint, OhioHealth is one of the most significant health systems in and around central Ohio. It uses its market power to extract restrictive contract provisions and high prices from payors. Those provisions, which include restrictions on tiered plans, narrow networks, steering, and price transparency, effectively prevent payors from offering consumers and employers the opportunity to pay less for healthcare at less expensive hospitals and providers. The restrictions also inhibit competition among hospitals because they limit the opportunity of hospitals with lower prices to gain more patient volume. Because the restrictions deter OhioHealth's competitors from competing by reducing prices, they protect OhioHealth from pressure to reduce its own prices. This inhibited price competition raises the cost of health insurance and results in patients and employers paying more for essential healthcare.
The proposed Final Judgment provides an effective and appropriate remedy for the competitive harms arising out of OhioHealth's alleged conduct. The proposed Final Judgment has several components, which OhioHealth agreed to abide by pending entry of the Final Judgment, as the Court ordered in the Stipulation and Order entered on July 2, 2026. (Dkt. 31).
First, the proposed Final Judgment voids any and all language in OhioHealth's contracts with payors that prohibits, deters, prevents, or penalizes steering, steered plans, or transparency. Second, the proposed Final Judgment prevents OhioHealth from seeking or obtaining new contract provisions that would prohibit, prevent, or penalize steering, steered plans, or transparency. Third, the proposed Final Judgment prohibits OhioHealth from penalizing or retaliating against payors that engage (or are planning to engage) in steering, offer steered plans, or provide price transparency to their members. Fourth, the proposed Final Judgment prohibits OhioHealth from requiring that it be included in the most-preferred tier of any benefit plan offered by payors. Finally, the proposed Final Judgment provides for the Court to appoint a monitor who will serve for five years and will have the power to investigate and report on OhioHealth's compliance with the terms of the Final Judgment.
Together, these requirements of the proposed Final Judgment will preserve competition for the sale of inpatient general acute care hospital services to commercial payors and their members in Ohio.
IV. Summary of Public Comments and the United States' Response
The United States received four comments about the proposed Final Judgment. The comments do not question the adequacy of the proposed Final Judgment to remedy the detrimental effects of OhioHealth's restrictions on steering and transparency that are at the core of the Sherman Act claim. Rather, each of the four comments relates to facts or events
(
printed page 69868)
outside the scope of the conduct challenged under the Sherman Act claim and therefore are outside the scope of the Court's Tunney Act review.
a. General Comments About OhioHealth's Market Power
Two commenters expressed concerns about OhioHealth's possession and exertion of market power to harm various stakeholders including patients, employees, and others in the communities surrounding their hospitals.
First, the United States received a comment from the Ohio Nurses Association (“Association”). The Association wrote to request that the United States “broaden its scrutiny of OhioHealth's conduct and the impact its market power is having on patients and communities throughout [the] state.” (Exhibit A, TC-001). Specifically, the Association cites to OhioHealth's recent closure of its inpatient maternity services at Grady Memorial Hospital as an example of harm caused by OhioHealth's “growing market power.”
Id.
Second, the United States received a comment from a current employee of OhioHealth voicing concerns about OhioHealth's treatment of employees, patients, and the community. The employee described the failure of OhioHealth to make market-rate salary adjustments. They also shared the Association's concern about OhioHealth's closure of the Labor and Delivery Unit at Grady Memorial Hospital. (Exhibit A, TC-003).
These comments do not discuss OhioHealth's contract restrictions on steering and price transparency in the relevant market that were challenged in the Sherman Act claim or how the proposed remedy is allegedly inadequate to resolve the competitive harm that is caused by those restrictions. Because these comments do not relate to whether the proposed Final Judgment reasonably addresses the harms alleged in the Complaint, they are beyond the scope of the Court's review under the Tunney Act and do not provide a basis for rejecting the proposed Final Judgment.
See U.S. Airways,
38 F. Supp. 3d at 76 (“[T]he Court's role under the [Tunney Act] is limited to reviewing the remedy in relationship to the violations that the United States has alleged in its Complaint.” (internal citation omitted)).
b. Specific Comment About OhioHealth's Contracting Practices
The United States received one comment that requested the inclusion of an “explicit ban on all-or-nothing contracting provisions” in the proposed Final Judgment. (Exhibit A, TC-002). In the commenter's view, the lack of an explicit ban on all-or-nothing contracting could “leave a critical loophole that allows dominant systems to continue leveraging market power to the detriment of Ohio employers, workers, and patients.” (
Id.
).
The United States' Sherman Act claim challenges only OhioHealth's steering and transparency restrictions. The proposed Final Judgment provides effective relief for the challenged conduct by banning all present and future steering and transparency restrictions and enjoining any action that would penalize steering.
A separate ban on all-or-nothing contracting is unwarranted to resolve the United States' claim. The United States' claim does not challenge OhioHealth's all-or-nothing contracting as a violation of Section 1 of the Sherman Act. Rather, the Complaint alleges as a matter of fact that OhioHealth engages in all-or-nothing contracting, which can reflect the existence of market power. However, the Sherman Act claim challenges OhioHealth's steering and transparency restrictions themselves, not the all-or-nothing contracting. If OhioHealth were to impose an all-or-nothing contracting requirement that prevents a Payor from steering, that would violate the proposed Final Judgment.
Moreover, the proposed Final Judgment includes multiple reservations of rights explicitly stating that (1) if the proposed Final Judgment fails to fully redress the violations alleged in the Complaint, then the United States may re-open the proceeding and seek additional relief; and (2) the proposed Final Judgment terminates only the claims stated in the Complaint and does not affect other charges or claims the United States or the State of Ohio may file. (Dkt. 29-2 at 17, 19). If in the future the United States learns that OhioHealth's all-or-nothing contracting practices result in anticompetitive harm, the United States may investigate the conduct, and if warranted, bring an enforcement action against OhioHealth for that conduct.
c. Blood Cancer United's Comment
On September 21, 2026, the United States received a comment from Blood Cancer United, in which the organization wrote that it “agree[s] that the proposed Final Judgment achieves all or substantially all of the relief the United States would have obtained through litigation, while avoiding the time, expense, and uncertainty of a full trial on the merits.” (Exhibit A, TC-004). Blood Cancer United expressed concerns primarily about the general consolidation of healthcare and urged lawmakers and enforcement agencies to prevent systems like OhioHealth from obtaining market power in the first place and thus being able to impose the contract restrictions alleged in the Complaint. These concerns are not related to OhioHealth's contract restrictions on steering and price transparency in the relevant market and are therefore beyond the scope of the Court's review under the Tunney Act.
Similarly, in relation to the price transparency restrictions challenged in the Complaint, Blood Cancer United wrote that the United States could broaden the scope of its relief by requiring that OhioHealth “disclose the availability of financial assistance on its main website” and provide “notice about financial assistance with a paper copy of the application.”
Id.
at 4. However, the price transparency restrictions challenged in the Complaint relate to payors' efforts to increase transparency about prices of healthcare services. The Complaint did not challenge OhioHealth's own disclosure requirements. Therefore, the additional relief recommended by Blood Cancer United falls outside the scope of the proposed Final Judgment and thus beyond the scope of the Court's review under the Tunney Act.
Finally, the organization commended the appointment of a monitor but suggested that a longer monitorship may be necessary to “provide better oversight and foster institutional reform.”
Id.
The United States believes that a term of five years is sufficient to ensure OhioHealth's compliance with the proposed Final Judgment. However, the proposed Final Judgment does include a reservation that the United States, in its sole discretion, may determine a different period is appropriate. (Dkt. 29-2 at 13).
The concerns expressed by Blood Cancer United are either outside the scope of the harm alleged in the Complaint or are already addressed in the proposed Final Judgment. As the organization itself agrees, the proposed Final Judgment effectively relieves the harm of the antitrust violations alleged in the Complaint.
V. Conclusion
After careful consideration of the public comments, the United States continues to believe the proposed Final Judgment provides an effective and appropriate remedy for the antitrust violations alleged in the Complaint and is therefore in the public interest. The United States will move this Court to
(
printed page 69869)
enter the proposed Final Judgment after this response and the public comments are published in the
Federal Register
as required by
15 U.S.C. 16(d)
.
Dated: November 2, 2026
Respectfully submitted,

AGENCY:
Maritime Administration (MARAD), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking and request for comments.
SUMMARY:
This document proposes procedures for the processing of applications for the licensing of deepwater ports. The proposed rule reflects the transfer of deepwater port license application processing management under the Deepwater Port Act from the United States Coast Guard (USCG) to MARAD. Pursuant to the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2026 (2026 NDAA), MARAD is the Federal lead agency for purposes of the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (NEPA) for all deepwater port license applications. USCG responsibility for authorities pertaining to design, construction, equipment, operation of deepwater ports, and navigational safety are not affected by the 2026 NDAA statutory changes, or this proposed rule and will continue to be administered by USCG.
DATES:
Comments should be filed on or before January 4, 2027. Late comments will be considered to the extent practicable.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments identified by DOT Docket Number MARAD-2026-0728 by any of the following methods:
Federal eRulemaking Portal:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
Search for the above DOT Docket Number and follow the instructions for submitting comments.
Mail/Hand-Delivery/Courier:
Docket Management Facility, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Room W12-140, Washington, DC 20590. If you would like to know that your comments reached the facility, please enclose a stamped, self-addressed postcard or envelope. The Docket Management Facility is open 9:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., Monday through Friday, except on Federal holidays.
Note:
MARAD recommends that you include your name, mailing address, email address, or telephone number in the body of your document so that MARAD can contact you if we have questions regarding your submission. If you submit your input by mail or hand-delivery, it must be submitted in an unbound format, no larger than 8
                        1/2
                         by 11 inches, single-sided, suitable for copying and electronic filing. All submissions received should include the agency name and “DOT Docket Number” or Regulation Identifier Number (RIN) for this rulemaking.
Instructions:
All comments received will be posted without change to the docket at
https://www.regulations.gov
,
including any personal information provided. For detailed instructions on submitting comments and additional information on the rulemaking process, see the section entitled Public Participation.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Efrain Lopez, Office of Deepwater Port Licensing and Port Conveyance by phone at (202) 495-8867, email:
efrain.lopez@dot.gov
,
or mail addressed to U.S. Department of Transportation, Maritime Administration, MAR-530, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590. If you have questions about viewing the docket, call the Docket Management Facility, telephone: (800) 647-5527.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Electronic Access and Filing
As required by
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4)
, this document, including a summary of the rule, and all comments may be viewed online through the Federal eRulemaking portal at
https://www.regulations.gov
.
An electronic copy of this document may also be downloaded by accessing the Office of the Federal Register's home page at
https://www.federalregister.gov
.
Privacy Act information.
Anyone can search the electronic form of all comments received into any of our dockets by the name of the individual submitting the comment (or signing the comment, if submitted on behalf of an association, business, labor union, or other entity). For information on DOT's compliance with the Privacy Act, please visit
https://www.transportation.gov/​privacy
.
Background
MARAD and USCG have worked collaboratively to process Deepwater Port applications since the agencies began jointly processing applications in 1997. However, as required by the 2026 NDAA, MARAD and USCG are realigning their review responsibilities, with MARAD leading the application review process and conducting NEPA reviews of project applications.
The Deepwater Port Act of 1974, as amended (DWPA,
33 U.S.C. 1501
et seq.
), establishes a licensing system for the ownership, construction, and operation of oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) deepwater ports located beyond State seaward boundaries. Deepwater ports are fixed or floating facilities used as terminals to transfer oil or natural gas to or from shore via sub-sea pipeline to load or unload onto carrier vessels for the import or export of oil or LNG.
The DWPA vests licensing authority in the Secretary of Transportation. Shortly after the enactment of the statute, the Secretary delegated the authority to process applications and issue regulations to USCG, but reserved the authority to issue, transfer, and amend deepwater port licenses (
40 FR 43901
,
43906
(Sept. 24, 1975)). As a result, USCG issued DWPA implementing regulations at
33 CFR parts 148
,
149
, and
150
(
40 FR 52339
,
52540
(Nov. 10, 1975)). In 1997, the Secretary delegated to MARAD the authority to work in coordination with USCG to process deepwater port applications (
62 FR 11382
,
11383
(Mar. 12, 1997)). In 2003, the Secretary delegated to the Maritime Administrator the Secretary's authority to issue, transfer, and amend deepwater port licenses (
68 FR 36496
,
36497
(June 18, 2003)). This delegation did not change the previous delegation of license processing functions to USCG, and its authorities under the DWPA remained intact upon its transfer to the Department of Homeland Security
(
printed page 69769)
under sections 888 and 1512(d) of the Homeland Security Act (
Pub. L. 107-296
, Sections 888 and 1512 (Nov. 25, 2002)). Section 7342 of subtitle E of title LXXIII of the 2026 NDAA (
Pub. L. 119-60
(Dec. 18, 2025)) amended the DWPA by designating MARAD as the Federal lead agency for the purposes of NEPA compliance and directed the Commandant of the USCG to transfer its authorities under
33 CFR part 148
to the Secretary of Transportation and to retain responsibility for authorities pertaining to the design, construction, equipment, and operation of deepwater ports and navigational safety.
Discussion
Pursuant to Section 7342 of the 2026 NDAA,
33 CFR part 148
functions, as well as rulemaking authority, were transferred from the USCG to the Secretary of Transportation. Executive Order (E.O.) 14154,
Unleashing American Energy,
sets a national policy for the efficient administration of licensing and permitting regimes that govern the development of domestic energy resources and directs Federal agencies to review their regulations and processes to promote this policy. Since passage of the 2026 NDAA, MARAD and USCG have evaluated the deepwater port licensing process considering decades of experience jointly reviewing license applications and determined that license application processing functions should be consolidated and realigned so that MARAD, the license issuing agency, would lead the application review process for deepwater port licenses. MARAD and the USCG have concluded that the consolidation and realignment of processing functions would help clarify and streamline the application review process, leading to greater efficiency in the issuance of licensing decisions.
Under the proposed realignment, MARAD would serve as the lead agency for conducting environmental review of applications under
33 U.S.C. 1504(f)
and NEPA, manage application processing, and assume rulemaking authority over application processing under
33 U.S.C. 1504(a)
. USCG would retain responsibility for authorities pertaining to risk and consequence assessments (currently
33 CFR 148.105(y)
) and navigational safety, design, construction, equipment, and operation of deepwater ports (
33 CFR parts 149
and
150
). To carry out this realignment, MARAD proposes to adopt the provisions of
33 CFR part 148
pertaining to the application processing and environmental review criteria as well as revisions to Part 148 proposed by USCG's Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (2015 NPRM) published on April 9, 2015 (
80 FR 19118
), which were intended to clarify existing application requirements.
MARAD conducts environmental reviews for deepwater port applications consistent with the Supreme Court's decision in
Seven County Infrastructure Coalition
v.
Eagle County, Colorado
and its progeny.
[
1
]
Consistent with the requirements of
42 U.S.C. 4336a(b)
, if a proposed action will require action by more than one Federal agency, MARAD and the cooperating agencies evaluate the proposal in a single environmental document. MARAD proposes to add a new section 248.44,
How will environmental reviews be conducted?,
to reflect the agency's approach to conducting these reviews. MARAD seeks comment on whether further changes to the regulatory text are needed consistent with the Court's decision in
Seven County.
Public Participation
MARAD encourages public participation in this rulemaking by submitting comments and related materials.
How long do I have to submit comments?
MARAD provides a 60-day comment period for this proposed rulemaking. Comments must be submitted on or before the date indicated in the
DATES
section at the beginning of this document.
How do I prepare and submit comments?
Comments may be submitted to the docket electronically by logging onto the Docket Management System website at
https://www.regulations.gov
,
searching for this rulemaking by the DOT Docket Number listed above and following the online instructions for submitting comments. MARAD will also accept comments via mail or hand-delivery to the Docket Management Facility at the address given above under
ADDRESSES
.
All comments, no matter how they are received, will be posted to the docket following DOT rulemaking procedures. To ensure that your comments are correctly filed in the docket, please include the DOT Docket Number shown at the beginning of this document in your comments.
Please note that pursuant to the Data Quality Act, for substantive data to be relied upon and used by the agency, it must meet the information quality standards set forth in the OMB and DOT Data Quality Act guidelines. Accordingly, MARAD encourages you to consult the guidelines in preparing your comments. OMB's guidelines may be accessed at
https://www.opm.gov/​information-management/​information-quality-guidelines/​
.
DOT's guidelines may be accessed at
https://www.transportation.gov/​sites/​dot.gov/​files/​docs/​regulations/​513/​dot-information-quality-guidelines-2019.pdf
.
How can I be sure that my comments were received?
For electronic comments:
Comments submitted electronically at
https://www.regulations.gov
will be reflected on the docket typically within three business days.
For mailed comments:
If you wish for the Docket Management Facility to notify you upon receipt of your comments, enclose a self-addressed, stamped postcard in the envelope containing your comments. Upon receiving your comments, Docket Management will return the postcard by mail. All comments received by the Docket Management Facility will be posted to the electronic docket typically within five business days.
How do I submit confidential business information?
Confidential business information (CBI) is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments to the rule contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this rule, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission that constitutes CBI as “PROPIN” to indicate it contains proprietary information and make your submission via email to
Rulemakings.MARAD@dot.gov
.
MARAD will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will be redacted or omitted in their entirety, as appropriate, from the public docket of this rule. In addition, to assist our proper management of your CBI/PROPIN comment submission, MARAD recommends that you submit a version of your confidential comment from which you have redacted the sensitive information. Doing so will assist
(
printed page 69770)
MARAD in posting a redacted version of your comment to the docket and it will allow for MARAD to rely on the substantive content of your comment in developing the rulemaking. A redacted submission will also assist any review under a relevant FOIA request where the submission may be considered responsive information. Any comments MARAD receives that are not specifically designated as CBI/PROPIN will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
May I submit comments anonymously?
All comments on this rulemaking, whether submitted to
regulations.gov
or by mail or hand-delivery to the Docket Management Facility at DOT, may be made anonymously. It is not necessary to identify yourself when submitting comments on the rule. Because public comments are generally posted to the public docket without change, MARAD recommends that information of a personal nature that the commenter (or the involved party, if not the commenter) does not want to be made public not be submitted in response to the request for public comment on this rule. MARAD notes that under the FOIA, information is exempt from public disclosure if disclosure would constitute a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy. If your comments contain personal information relevant or responsive to this rule but disclosure of the information would be a clearly unwarranted invasion of personal privacy, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as confidential.
Anonymous submissions containing confidential information should be sent to MARAD via email to
Rulemakings.MARAD@dot.gov
with the term “CONFIDENTIAL” in the subject heading and on each page containing confidential information. In addition, to assist our proper management of your comment submission, MARAD recommends that you submit a version of your confidential comment from which you have redacted the confidential information. This will allow MARAD to post the redacted version of your comment to the docket without attribution to you or your organization and allow MARAD to rely on the substantive content in developing the rulemaking. It will also assist any review under a relevant FOIA request where your submission may be considered responsive information.
Will the agency consider late comments?
MARAD will consider all comments received via
regulations.gov
and mail or hand-delivery to the Docket Management Facility before the close of business on the comment closing date indicated above under
DATES
. To the extent practicable, MARAD will also consider comments received after that date.
How can I read the comments submitted by other people?
You may read comments in the docket for this rulemaking online by going to
https://www.regulations.gov
and following the instructions for accessing the docket or by searching for the DOT Docket Number available at the beginning of this document and under the
ADDRESSES
section. You may also read physical copies of the publicly available comments received by the Docket Management Facility at the address given above under
ADDRESSES
. The hours of the Docket Management Facility office are indicated above in the same section.
Please note that, even after the comment closing date, MARAD will continue to file relevant information in the docket as it becomes available. Further, some people may submit late comments. Accordingly, MARAD recommends that you periodically check the docket for new material.
Regulatory Analyses and Notices
Executive Order 12866
This proposed rule has been determined to be “significant” pursuant to Section 3(f) of
E.O. 12866
and was therefore reviewed by the Office of Management and Budget (OMB).
Need for the Regulation
Section 7342 of 2026 NDAA designated MARAD as the Federal lead agency for the purposes of NEPA compliance and directed the Commandant of the USCG to transfer its authorities under
33 CFR part 148
, governing the deepwater port license application process and environmental review, to the Secretary of Transportation and to retain responsibility for authorities pertaining to the design, construction, equipment, and operation of deepwater ports and navigational safety. The proposed regulation would largely adopt and replace the provisions of
33 CFR part 148
pertaining to deepwater port license application submittal and processing and environmental criteria for application review. MARAD and USCG have concluded that the consolidation and realignment of application processing functions under MARAD would streamline the application review process, leading to greater efficiency in the issuance of licensing decisions in furtherance of
E.O. 14154
's policy for the efficient administration of licensing and permitting regimes that govern the development of domestic energy resources and directs Federal agencies to review their regulations and processes to promote this policy
Baseline
Under the no action baseline, applicants for deepwater port licenses are subject to USCG regulations found at
33 CFR part 148
, rather than regulations issued by MARAD.
Costs
This proposed rule would update existing MARAD administrative responsibilities reflecting the transfer of deepwater port NEPA review and compliance functions from USCG to MARAD.
NEPA responsibilities for deepwater port license applications were transferred from USCG to MARAD by statute. As a result, the NPRM does not impose new or additional NEPA compliance requirements or costs on applicants for deepwater port licenses; rather, the proposed rule would simply reassign Federal responsibilities with regard to NEPA review. Although there would likely be transactional and adminstrative adjustments concerning correspondence,
e.g.,
interacting with new points of contact and familiarization with MARAD's internet site concerning NEPA requirements, the adjustments are expected to be minor and temporary because MARAD is adopting USCG's regulations in
33 CFR part 148
. Additionally, MARAD proposes to adopt clarifying amendments proposed by USCG's April 9, 2015, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (2015 NPRM) (
80 FR 19118
), which are not expected to result in increased regulatory burdens on applicants. See the
Section-by-Section Analysis
for additional information. MARAD expects that this proposed rule would result in improved efficiency and clarity regarding the permitting process.
Consolidating the application processing and NEPA review within MARAD right-sizes inter-agency communications and reviews, streamlining the processing of operators' applications by the agencies. This proposed rule also provides specific administrative flexibilities and relief. It replaces previous agency-driven extensions with a process where timelines are suspended only upon request by the applicant when responding to additional information requests. The rule also allows applicants to submit existing hydrographic and
(
printed page 69771)
engineering geological survey data collected within the previous 5 years (or longer with MARAD approval) rather than forcing new, expensive offshore surveys. It also amends
33 CFR 148.115
to require only one printed copy and one electronic copy, eliminating multi-copy physical filing burdens (currently multiple copies in different formats to the USCG, MARAD, and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers). In addition, the proposed rule removes unused regulatory definitions and eliminates obsolete procedures (such as Adjacent Coastal State designation petitions under
33 CFR 148.217
that were repealed by statute).
MARAD is unable to estimate the expected cost savings for operators. MARAD requests comment on the potential direct savings operators may experience based on compliance costs, applications processing, and other aspects of this proposed rule.
Costs to MARAD consist of the incremental monetary and non-monetary expenses that would be incurred as MARAD undertakes the responsibilities mandated by the 2026 NDAA and reflected in the proposed regulation. The costs include (but are not limited to) application completeness review, attendance at public meetings/hearings, government travel costs, and development of the NEPA and other environmental documents. Although MARAD expects that administrative efficiency would result in a reduction in these costs, it is unable to estimate the amount that would be saved.
Transfers
The DWPA requires applicants to remit a a nonrefundable application fee (with the amount established by regulation) and to reimburse the government for all costs in processing applications (see
33 U.S.C. 1504(h)(1)
). Current USCG regulations at
33 CFR 148.125
set the application fee at $350,000, and the proposed regulation would maintain the same fee level. Due to the reimbursement requirement, however, the total cost to the Government of processing applications would continue to effectively be borne by the applicants and are not expected to change as a result of the transfer of responsibilities from USCG.
Benefits
The elimination of duplicative agency application processing functions, resulting in reduced statutory processing cost reimbursement obligations borne by applicants, is in the national interest and consistent with national security, energy sufficiency, environmental quality, and other national policy goals and objectives. The benefits of this NPRM would ensure that deepwater port applications are reviewed and processed, and a license determination is made, all within one Department. With this new authority, MARAD would continue to work to ensure that deepwater ports, as United States maritime transportation systems, are well designed, safe, secure, and approved in a timely manner.
Summary
The proposed rule reflects the transfer of deepwater port license application processing management under the DWPA from USCG to MARAD. USCG responsibility for authorities pertaining to the design, equipment, construction, operation of deepwater ports, and navigational safety are not affected by this NPRM and would continue to be administered by USCG. The NPRM provides procedures for processing applications, including NEPA review, for the licensing of deepwater ports, which are any fixed or floating manmade structure other than a vessel, or any group of such structures, that are located beyond State seaward boundaries and that are used or intended for use as a port or terminal for the transportation, storage, or further handling of oil or natural gas for transportation to or from any State. The rule would clarify agency functions, eliminate duplicative interagency communication requirements, incorporate statutory changes, and allow both MARAD and USCG to focus exclusively on areas of core technical expertise.

(a) By delegation from the Secretary of Transportation, MARAD is authorized to process applications for the issuance, transfer, or amendment of licenses for the construction and operation of deepwater ports. Pursuant to that authority, MARAD is responsible for the following:

e.g.,
Environmental Assessments, Environmental Impact Statement) for each deepwater port license application. The United States Coast Guard (USCG) is responsible for certain matters relating to navigation safety and security, engineering and safety standards, and deepwater port operations;
(2) Issuing the Record of Decision (ROD) to announce whether a license application is approved, approved with conditions, or denied, and for issuing, revoking, and reinstating deepwater port licenses;
(3) Approving fees charged by Adjacent Coastal States; and
(4) Administering certain matters relating to international policy, civil actions, and suspension or termination of licenses.
(b) By delegation from the Secretary of Transportation, the Administrator of the Pipeline Hazardous Materials and Safety Administration (PHMSA) is authorized to carry out the functions vested in the Secretary under section 21 of the Act relating to the safe construction, operation, and maintenance of pipelines associated with deepwater ports.
(c) The Secretary of the Interior is responsible for determining the fair market rental value of the subsoil and seabed of the Outer Continental Shelf of the United States to be used by the deepwater port, including, but not limited to, the fair market rental value of the right-of-way necessary for the pipeline segment of the port located on such subsoil and seabed. Any proposed subsurface storage of oil and gas in the submerged lands of the Outer Continental Shelf is also subject to the review and approval of the Secretary of the Interior. To minimize potential impacts to existing facilities and protect the development potential of nearby oil, gas, and mineral resources, the Department of the Interior should also be involved in the site selection process.
(d) USCG, Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, U.S. Army Corps of Engineers, and other Federal agencies are designated by the Act as cooperating agencies to provide support to MARAD in its review and evaluation of deepwater port license applications including any required environmental review.
§ 248.4
How are terms used in this part defined?
(a)
Accommodation module
means a module with one or more modular accommodation spaces that are individually contracted and may be used for one or more facilities.
(b)
Act
means the Deepwater Port Act of 1974, as amended (codified at
33 U.S.C. 1501
et seq.
).
(c)
Adjacent Coastal State
means any coastal State which:
(
printed page 69776)
(1) Would be directly connected by pipeline to a deepwater port, as proposed in an application; or
(2) Would be located within 15 nautical miles of any such proposed deepwater port.
(d)
Affiliate
means a person or company that:
(1) Owns a direct or indirect interest of more than three percent in an applicant;
(2) Offers to finance, manage, construct, or operate the applicant's deepwater port to any significant degree;
(3) Owns or controls an applicant or an entity under paragraphs (1) or (2) of this definition; or
(4) Owns or is controlled by, or is under common ownership of, an applicant or an entity under paragraphs (1), (2), or (3) of this definition.
(e)
Applicant
means a person that proposes to own, construct, and operate a deepwater port and applies for a license under this part.
(f)
Application
means an application submitted under this part for a license to own, construct, and operate a deepwater port.
(g)
Approved
means approved by MARAD unless otherwise specified.
(h)
Barrel
means 42 U.S. gallons (approximately 159 liters) at atmospheric pressure and 60 °F.
(i)
Citizen of the United States
means:
(1) Any person who is a United States citizen by law, birth, or naturalization;
(2) Any State, State agency, or group of States; or
(3) Any corporation, partnership, or other association:
(i) That is organized under the laws of any State;
(ii) Whose president, chairman of the board of directors, and general partners or their equivalents, are persons described in paragraph (1) of this definition; and
(iii) That has no more of its directors who are not persons described in paragraph (1) of this definition than constitute a minority of the number required for a quorum to conduct the business of the board of directors.
(j)
Coastal environment
means the coastal waters including the lands in and under those waters, internal waters, and the adjacent shorelines including waters in and under those shorelines. The term includes, but is not limited to:
(1) Transitional and intertidal areas, bays, lagoons, salt marshes, estuaries, and beaches;
(2) Fish, wildlife, and other living resources of those waters and lands; and
(3) The recreational and scenic values of those lands, waters, and resources.
(k)
Coastal State
means a State of the United States in or bordering the Atlantic, Pacific, or Arctic Oceans or the Gulf of America.
(l)
Confined space
means a space that may contain a dangerous atmosphere, including a space that:
(1) Has poor natural ventilation, for example a space with limited openings, such as a cofferdam or double bottom tank; or
(2) Is not designed for continuous occupancy by personnel.
(m)
Construction
means the supervising, inspecting, actual building, and all other activities incidental to the building, repairing, or expanding of a deepwater port or any of its components. The term includes, but is not limited to, fabrication, laying of pipe, pile driving, bulk heading, alterations, modifications, and additions to the deepwater port.
(n)
Control
means the direct or indirect power to determine the policy, business practices, or decision-making process of another person, whether by stock or other ownership interest, by representation on a board of directors or similar body, by contract or other agreement with stockholders or others, or otherwise.
(o)
Crude oil
means a mixture of hydrocarbons that exists in the liquid phase in natural underground reservoirs, and remains liquid at atmospheric pressure after passing through surface separating facilities, and includes:
(1) Liquids technically defined as crude oil;
(2) Small amounts of hydrocarbons that exist in the gaseous phase in natural underground reservoirs but are liquid at atmospheric pressure after being recovered from oil well (casing head) gas in lease separators; and
(3) Small amounts of non-hydrocarbons produced with the oil.
(p)
Dangerous atmosphere
means an atmosphere that:
(1) May expose personnel to the risk of death, incapacitation, injury, or acute illness; or
(2) May impair ability to escape from the atmosphere unaided.
(q)
Deepwater port
means any fixed or floating manmade structures other than a vessel, or any group of structures, located beyond State seaward boundaries that are used or are intended for use as a port or terminal for the transportation, storage, or further handling of oil or natural gas for transportation to or from any State, except as otherwise provided in the Deepwater Port Act of 1974, as amended, and for other uses not inconsistent with the purposes of the Deepwater Port Act, including transportation of oil or natural gas from the United States OCS, and:
(1) Includes all components and equipment, including pipelines, pumping stations, service platforms, buoys, mooring lines, and similar facilities, to the extent that they are located seaward of the high-water mark;
(2) Includes, in the case of natural gas, all components and equipment, including pipelines, pumping or compressor stations, service platforms, buoys, mooring lines, and similar facilities which are proposed or approved for construction and operation as part of the deepwater port, to the extent that they are located seaward of the high-water mark and do not include interconnecting facilities; and
(3) Must be considered a “new source” for purposes of the Clean Air Act, as amended (codified at
42 U.S.C. 7401
et seq.
), and the Federal Water Pollution Control Act, as amended (codified at
33 U.S.C. 1251
et seq.
).
(r)
District commander
means an officer who commands a USCG district described in
33 CFR ch. I
, subch. NN, or that individual's authorized representative.
(s)
Emergency medical technician
means a person trained and certified to appraise and initiate the administration of emergency care for victims of trauma or acute illness before or during transportation of the victims to a health care facility via ambulance, aircraft, or vessel.
(t)
Engineering geological survey
means a detailed geological analysis of seabed soil samples performed to determine the physical composition—for example the mineral content—and structural integrity for the installation of offshore components and structures.
(u)
Governor
means the Governor of a State, or the person designated by State law to exercise the powers granted to the Governor under the Act.
(v)
Lease block
means an area established either by the Secretary of the Interior under
43 U.S.C. 1334
, or by a State under
43 U.S.C. 1311
.
(w)
License
means a license issued under this part to own, construct, and operate a deepwater port.
(x)
Licensee
means a citizen of the United States holding a valid license for the ownership, construction, and operation of a deepwater port that was issued, transferred, or renewed under this subchapter.
(y)
Marine environment
includes:
(1) The coastal environment, waters of the contiguous zone, the Exclusive Economic Zone, and the high seas;
(2) Fish, wildlife, and other living resources of those waters; and
(
printed page 69777)
(3) The recreational and scenic values of those waters and resources.
(z)
Marine site
means the area in which the deepwater port is located, including the safety zone and all areas seaward of the high-water mark in which associated components and equipment of the deepwater port are located.
(aa)
Maritime Administration
or
MARAD
means the Administrator of the Maritime Administration or that person's designee(s) at 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.
(bb)
Metering platform
means a manned or unmanned platform consisting of either a fixed or floating structure that serves as an interchange site for measuring the rate of transfer of natural gas between vessels and pipelines.
(cc)
Mile
means nautical mile.
(dd)
Natural gas
means either natural gas, unmixed, or any mixture of natural or artificial gas, including compressed or liquefied natural gas.
(ee)
Natural gas liquid
means liquid hydrocarbons associated with or extracted from natural gas, for example ethane, propane and butane extracted from natural gas.
(ff)
No anchoring area
or
NAA
means a routing measure comprising an area within defined limits where anchoring is hazardous or could result in unacceptable damage to the marine environment. Anchoring in a no-anchoring area should be avoided by all vessels or certain classes of vessels, except in case of immediate danger to the vessel or the person on board.
(gg)
Oil
means petroleum, crude oil, and any substance refined from petroleum or crude oil.
(hh)
Person
means an individual, a public or private corporation, a partnership or other association, or a government entity.
(ii)
Personnel
means individuals who are employed by licensees, operators, contractors, or subcontractors, and who are on a deepwater port because of their employment.
(jj)
Pipeline
means all parts of those physical facilities through which oil or gas moves in transportation, including pipe, valves, and other appurtenances.
(kk)
Platform
means a fixed or floating structure that rests on or is embedded in the seabed or moored in place and that has floors or decks where an activity or specific functions may be carried out.
(ll)
Reconnaissance hydrographic survey
means a scientific study of fresh and saltwater bodies, currents and water content, cultural resources, seabed soils, and subsea conditions. A visual representation of the survey findings is normally depicted on a chart of the examined area.
(mm)
Routing system
means any system of one or more vessel routes or routing measures aimed at reducing the risk of casualties. It includes traffic separation schemes, two-way routes, recommended tracks, areas to be avoided, no anchoring areas, inshore traffic zones, roundabouts, precautionary areas and deepwater routes.
(nn)
Safety zone
means a safety zone established around a deepwater port and extending up to 500 meters (approximately 1,640 feet) around the deepwater port, measured from each point on its outer edge or from its construction site, except as authorized by generally accepted international standards or as recommended by the International Maritime Organization but not interfering with the use of recognized sea lanes.
(oo)
State
means a State of the United States, the District of Columbia, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or a territory or possession of the United States.
(pp)
Support vessel
means a vessel working for a licensee at a deepwater port or cleared by a licensee to service a tanker calling at a deepwater port, and includes a:
(1) Tug;
(2) Line-handling boat;
(3) Crew boat;
(4) Supply vessel;
(5) Bunkering vessel;
(6) Barge; or
(7) Other similar vessel.
(qq)
Survival craft
means a craft described in
33 CFR ch. I
, subch. NN.
(rr)
Tanker
means a vessel that calls at a deepwater port to load or unload oil or natural gas.
(ss)
Vessel
means every description of watercraft, including non-displacement craft (
e.g.,
wing-in-ground (WIG) craft, seaplanes) capable of being used, as a means of transportation on or through the water.
B—Application for a License
§ 248.5
What must I include in my application?
(a)
General.
For each applicant, affiliate, and consultant, the application must include the following:
(1) The name, address, telephone number, citizenship, and principal business activity of the applicant and its affiliates;
(2) The name, address, and principal business activity of each subsidiary, division of the applicant, or its affiliates that participated in the decision to apply for a license to build a deepwater port;
(3) A description of how each affiliate is associated with the applicant, and of the ownership interest each affiliate has in the applicant;
(4) A list of the applicant's corporate officers and directors, and each affiliate that participated in the decision to apply for a license;
(5) A statement for each applicant or affiliate, providing complete and detailed information on any civil or criminal legal proceeding during the preceding 5 years that relates to, or that could materially affect, information in the license application; and
(6) A declaration by the applicant that neither the applicant nor its affiliates has engaged in any lobbying activities that are prohibited by
31 U.S.C. 1352
or any other applicable Federal anti-lobbying statute.
(b)
Experience in matters relating to deepwater ports.
(1) For each applicant, affiliate, and consultant, the application must include a description of the applicant's, affiliate's, and consultant's experience in offshore operations, particularly operations involving the transfer and storage of liquid cargo, and the loading and unloading of vessels; and
(2) For each affiliate that has a significant contract with the applicant for construction of the deepwater port, a description of that affiliate's experience in construction of marine terminal facilities, offshore structures, underwater pipelines, and seabed foundations, in addition to a description of other experiences that would bear on the affiliate's qualification to participate in the construction of a deepwater port.
(c)
Engineering firms.
Each engineering firm that will design the deepwater port or a portion of the port must provide the following information:
(1) Name;
(2) Address;
(3) Citizenship;
(4) Telephone number; and
(5) Qualifications.
(d)
