To date, ED has announced partnerships with six agencies designed to reduce federal education bureaucracy, improve the efficient delivery of federally funded programs and activities to better support students and families, and move closer to fulfilling the President's promise to return education to the states. The new partnerships with the Departments of Labor (DOL), Interior (DOI), Health and Human Services (HHS), State, Justice (DOJ), and Treasury have brought new thinking to the ED's grant programs. These partner agencies bring extensive experience in topics such as education choice scholarships, workforce readiness and career pathways, including Registered Apprenticeships and talent marketplaces; and Tribal self-determination. We are proposing amendments to the Secretary's Supplemental Priorities and Definitions as discussed in this notice to ensure our programs reflect the expertise our partner agencies offer, ensuring students are better positioned for success throughout their education journey and prepared to successfully enter, navigate, and advance in the workforce.
Additionally, after more than a year of visiting schools and communities across the country, hearing directly from students, educators, school leaders, State, Tribal and local officials, and other stakeholders about effective practices and emerging needs, and gaining practical experience implementing the existing Secretary's Supplemental Priorities and Definitions, ED has identified opportunities to
(
printed page 69738)
strengthen and refine the priorities. This experience has provided valuable insight into how the existing priorities operate in practice, where additional clarity or emphasis may be warranted, and where new or evolving policy areas should be addressed. Accordingly, ED has identified new topics for inclusion and aspects of the existing priorities and definitions that warrant revision to ensure that future implementation efforts reflect lessons learned, respond to developments in the education and workforce landscape, and remain closely aligned with the Administration's priorities.
Proposed Changes
We discuss the proposed changes to the priorities and definitions under the final notices to which they pertain. Generally, we do not address proposed changes that are technical or otherwise minor in effect.
Proposed Changes From Artificial Intelligence (AI) to Super Intelligence (SI)
Current Priorities and Definitions:
We finalized definitions of artificial intelligence (AI) and AI literacy in the Secretary's Supplemental Priority and Definitions on Advancing Artificial Intelligence in Education.
Proposed Priorities and Definitions:
We propose, with limited exceptions described in the next paragraph, to use the term “Super Intelligence” to replace “Artificial Intelligence” and use “SI” to replace “AI” in every use of the terms. This includes the following changes:
(1) proposing to rename the title of the notice from the “Notice of Final Priority and Definitions—Secretary's Supplemental Priority and Definitions on Advancing Artificial Intelligence in Education” to the “Notice of Final Priority and Definitions—Secretary's Supplemental Priority and Definitions on Advancing Super Intelligence in Education.”
(2) proposing to rename the title of the final priority from “Advancing Artificial Intelligence in Education” to “Advancing Super Intelligence in Education.”
(3) proposing to rename the definition of “Artificial Intelligence (AI)” to “Super Intelligence (SI).”
(4) proposing to rename the definition of “AI literacy” to “SI literacy.”
The exceptions to replacing “Artificial Intelligence” with “Super Intelligence” are in the definition of SI and in the title of the following document: “Department of Labor's Artificial Intelligence Literacy Framework.” The definition of SI includes reference to “artificial intelligence” therefore, we will continue to use “artificial intelligence” when referring to the definition of SI. Later in this notice we propose to add reference to a DOL document in the newly titled Priority on Advancing Super Intelligence in Education, and we describe our proposal and our reasons for doing so. This document and all references to it, will retain the title of “Department of Labor's Artificial Intelligence Literacy Framework.”
For the newly titled SI definition, we propose to adopt the definition of SI included in President Trump's Executive Order (E.O.) 14344 “Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence,” dated September 29, 2026, which says that SI means the technologies and systems encompassed by the term “artificial intelligence” as defined
15 U.S.C. 9401(3)
. The newly titled SI literacy definition would be revised to incorporate the importance of understanding how SI works and how to use SI tools effectively and responsibly.
Finally, we propose to add the definitions of SI and SI literacy to all uses of the terms in the Secretary's Supplemental Priorities on Evidence-Based Literacy, Educational Choice, and Returning Education to the States, the Secretary's Supplemental Priority on Meaningful Learning Opportunities, and the Secretary's Supplemental Priority on Career Pathways and Workforce Readiness.
Reasons:
On September 29, 2026, the President issued
E.O. 14434
(
91 FR 63129
) directing executive departments and agencies to replace the terms “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” with “Super Intelligence” and “SI” in official correspondence, public communications, policy documents, and other non-statutory documents.
E.O. 14344
explains that this terminology is intended to reflect the continuously advancing technological frontier and the expanding capabilities and applications of these technologies. Consistent with this direction, the Department proposes to update the terms used throughout the priorities and definitions by replacing references to “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” with “Super Intelligence” and “SI,” as discussed previously. These revisions align the priority with current Federal terminology and the Administration's direction for executive branch agencies while maintaining the substantive focus of the priority on preparing students and educators to understand, use, and benefit from these rapidly advancing technologies.
We also propose to adopt the definition of Super Intelligence from
E.O. 14344
. We believe this definition, as specified in
E.O. 14344
, is most appropriate because this definition provides terminology for implementing these priorities unless and until it is superseded by subsequent Presidential action consistent with applicable law or by an Act of Congress.
Consistent with this discussion, we propose to rename the definition of “AI literacy” to “SI literacy” and to revise the definition. The current definition of AI literacy means technical knowledge, durable skills, civic awareness, and future ready attitudes, including AI related ethical reasoning, critical social inquiry, interdisciplinary problem-solving, and creativity, required to thrive in a world influenced by AI. The definition also indicates that AI literacy enables learners to engage, create with, manage, and design AI, while critically evaluating its benefits, risks, and implications. In addition to replacing “AI” with “SI”, we propose to add to the definition the importance of understanding how SI works and how to use SI tools effectively and responsibly. We believe the amendment improves the clarity of the SI literacy definition and is necessary for promoting the appropriate integration of SI into education.
We propose to add the definitions of “SI” and “SI literacy” across all uses of the terms in the four notices proposed for revision in this proposed rule. Using common terminology and definitions across all of the supplemental priorities will help ensure consistency in understanding and implementation in ED's grant programs.
Proposed Changes to the Notice of Final Priorities and Definitions—Secretary's Supplemental Priorities and Definitions on Evidence-Based Literacy, Education Choice, and Returning Education to the States (
90 FR 43514
)
Changes to Priority Text
Current Priority:
Part (a) of the Expanding Education Choice priority focuses on increasing access to public charter schools and other innovative school models, including charter schools that have specific focus areas.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to revise part (a) to include technical, trade, and vocational schools in addition to public charter schools and other innovative school models; revise part (a)(i)(1) to expand the focus area on science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) to include super intelligence (SI), SI literacy, and cybersecurity; and revise part (a)(i)(2) to qualify that career and technical education includes programs that integrate pre-apprenticeship and Registered Apprenticeship pathways.
(
printed page 69739)
Reasons:
We propose to add technical, trade, and vocational schools to part (a) to emphasize these programs as important education and training options for students and families. Additionally, these options will help achieve our goal of ensuring that we prioritize access to demand-driven career pathways and workforce preparedness. We propose to add explicit reference to SI, SI literacy, and cybersecurity to part (a)(i)(1) to affirm these as important topics within STEM. And, we propose in part (a)(i)(2) to emphasize programs integrating pre-apprenticeships and Registered Apprenticeships pathways as valuable career and technical education choice options that are aligned with employer needs.
Current Priority:
Part (a)(iii) promotes projects that provide technical assistance to relevant parties about the establishment and operation of charter schools, including navigating State and local statutes and regulations. Part (f)(ii) promotes projects that provide families with assistance in understanding State and local requirements for homeschooling.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to revise (a)(iii) such that the provision of technical assistance includes support navigating Tribal statutes and regulations. And, we propose to redesignate (f)(i) and (ii) to be (g)(i) and (ii), and to revise the newly-designated (g)(ii) to include assistance with understanding Tribal requirements for homeschooling.
Reasons:
We propose these changes to ensure that the technical assistance contemplated by the priority fully reflects the range of legal and regulatory frameworks that may apply to charter schools and home-based education programs. As initially drafted, the priority expressly contemplated assistance with navigating applicable requirements but did not specifically identify Tribal statutes, regulations, or homeschooling requirements. Upon further review, we determined that expressly including Tribal requirements would provide greater clarity and ensure that the priority appropriately accounts for circumstances in which Tribal law or requirements may be relevant. Explicitly recognizing these requirements alongside other applicable legal and regulatory frameworks will help ensure that the technical assistance available under the priority is sufficiently comprehensive and responsive to the different jurisdictions and communities in which these educational options may operate.
Current Priority:
Part (c) of the Expanding Education Choice priority is specific to supporting dissemination of information related to school choice options.
Proposed Priority:
We are proposing to broaden part (c) to include two subparts. The current part (c) would be redesignated as (c)(ii). The newly proposed (c)(i) would encourage projects that provide technical assistance for education services available to students through scholarships supported by the about the Education Freedom Tax Credit (EFTC). We are proposing to revise the stem for part (c) to focus on the advancement and implementation of education choice options broadly.
Reasons:
The Department proposes to expand this priority to support the effective implementation of education choice initiatives, including the new EFTC. Providing technical assistance about education services available to students through scholarships supported by the EFTC will help ensure that eligible participants understand the opportunities available under the tax credit and how to access and implement these options. Broadening this priority will also allow the Department to support projects that strengthen the infrastructure necessary to expand educational freedom, empower families to make informed decisions, and increase access to education options that best meet students' individual needs.
Current Priority:
The current Expanding Education Choice priority does not include options for specific supports for student parents; talent marketplaces for postsecondary enrollment; or children and youth in foster care or kinship care, or their caregivers.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to add three new parts to the Expanding Education Choice priority and redesignate the current parts as appropriate. Newly designated part (f) would focus on expanding access to childcare and other supports for student-parents. A second part, newly designated part (j), would focus on expanding access to talent marketplaces and other best practices for postsecondary enrollment to include pre-apprenticeships and Registered Apprenticeships. A third part, newly designated part (o), would focus on children and youth in foster care or kinship care, or their caregivers, by promoting projects that improve educational stability and academic outcomes, supporting caregiver engagement in the education of children in their care, and expanding access to supports across the education spectrum from early childhood to postsecondary. Additionally, we propose to redesignate the other parts of this priority to conform with the proposed additions described above.
Reasons:
We propose to amend this priority to ensure that students and families have access to a broader range of educational pathways and supports that allow them to pursue an education aligned with their unique needs, circumstances, and career goals. These additions reflect feedback from our Federal partners at HHS and DOL, whose expertise and experience administering programs serving children, families, workers, and other populations helped identify additional ways in which the priority could more fully reflect the range of choices and supports that contribute to educational access and success.
In particular, HHS highlighted the importance of recognizing that meaningful education choice may depend on whether students and families can access the supports necessary to take advantage of those opportunities. This includes access to child care and other supports for student parents, as well as educational stability, caregiver engagement, and coordinated supports for children and youth in foster or kinship care. Incorporating these areas recognizes that students' individual circumstances can affect their ability to access and persist in educational opportunities and provides greater flexibility for ED, where consistent with applicable program authorities, to support projects that address those circumstances across the education continuum.
DOL similarly brought its expertise in workforce development and career-connected learning to identify opportunities to broaden the priority's treatment of postsecondary choice. In particular, DOL highlighted pre-apprenticeships and Registered Apprenticeships as additional pathways that can expand the range of high-quality postsecondary education and training options available to students. Including these pathways alongside talent marketplaces and approaches to postsecondary enrollment better reflects effective tools that connect jobseekers with employers and the variety of routes students may pursue to acquire skills, credentials, and experience that support their education and career goals. Taken together, these changes strengthen the priority by recognizing that expanding education choice involves not only increasing the number or type of educational options available, but also helping students and families access and successfully navigate those options. Drawing on the specialized expertise of
(
printed page 69740)
HHS and DOL allows ED to more comprehensively reflect the range of educational pathways and supports that may help students pursue opportunities best suited to their individual needs and goals.
Current Priority:
Part (f) of the Returning Education to the States priority includes an option for projects or proposals that are carried out by entities identified, designated, or endorsed by a Governor or a chief State education official.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to amend part (f) to include projects or proposals that are carried out by entities identified, designated, or endorsed by an Indian Tribe's highest ranking elected official.
Reasons:
In the current priority, we included Tribes, Tribal organizations and Tribal education agencies in the list of eligible entities (
i.e.,
part (g)) and noted ED's ability to preference support for Tribes using this part of the priority. However, in our use of part (f) in an FY 2026 grant competition we received questions about endorsements from Tribes. After considering the priority in light of these questions, we determined that it would be beneficial to add an Indian Tribe's highest ranking elected official to the existing parties (
i.e.,
Governor and chief State education official) in part (f). This proposed addition further recognizes the sovereignty of Tribal nations and importance of an applicant being identified, designated, or endorsed by a Tribe's highest ranking elected official for projects or proposals that will be carried out to support Native American children, youth, and families.
Changes to Definitions
Current Definitions:
The current set of definitions finalized with the Secretary's Supplemental Priorities on Evidence-Based Literacy, Educational Choice, and Returning Education to the States does not include definitions of SI, SI literacy, talent marketplaces, pre-apprenticeship or Registered Apprenticeship.
Proposed Definitions:
We propose to add definitions of SI, SI literacy, talent marketplaces, pre-apprenticeship, and Registered Apprenticeship.
Reasons:
We propose to add definitions of these terms to support the revised priorities proposed in this notice. The new definitions would apply to all uses of these terms in the Secretary's Supplemental Priorities on Evidence-Based Literacy, Educational Choice, and Returning Education to the States.
See our previous discussion about the terms SI and SI literacy for more information about the basis of these definitions.
We propose to add a definition of talent marketplace. The proposed definition is the same definition used in the Secretary's Supplemental Priority and Definitions on Career Pathways and Workforce Readiness published in the
Federal Register
on April 13, 2026. Using consistent definitions across all of the Secretary's Supplemental Priorities provides greater clarity for the public, reduces the potential for confusion or conflicting interpretations, and allows applicants and other stakeholders to operate from a common understanding of established terms.
We propose to add definitions of pre-apprenticeship and Registered Apprenticeship. The proposed definition of pre-apprenticeship is drawn from the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) Final Rule (
81 FR 56072
codified in
20 CFR 681.480
) and informed by DOL's
Framework for Effective Pre-Apprenticeships
in Training and Employment Notice No. 05-26. The proposed definition of Registered Apprenticeship is drawn from the National Apprenticeship Act (
29 U.S.C. Chapter 4C
) and
29 CFR parts 29
and
30
. Where possible, using consistent definitions across the Federal government provides greater clarity for the public, reduces the potential for confusion or conflicting interpretations across Federal programs, and allows applicants and other stakeholders to operate from a common understanding of established terms. Given ED's close partnership with DOL, as well as DOL's role in administering the national Registered Apprenticeship system, aligning with the existing Federal definitions of pre-apprenticeship and Registered Apprenticeship promotes consistency across agencies and ensures that references to pre-apprenticeship and Registered Apprenticeship have the same meaning across Federal education and workforce programs.
Proposed Changes to the Notice of Final Priority and Definitions—Secretary's Supplemental Priority and Definitions on Meaningful Learning Opportunities (
91 FR 6625
)
Current Priority:
Part (a)(i) of the priority focuses on strengthening core instruction through improving mathematics instruction. Part (a)(i) currently includes seven parts.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to add a new part (a)(i)(6) focused on aligning mathematics instruction with critical workplace math skills and real-world applications identified through engagement with national or regional employers, and re-number the current part (a)(i)(6) and succeeding parts in this paragraph.
Reasons:
We propose to add this part based on feedback from our partners at DOL, which highlighted the importance of strengthening the connection between mathematics instruction and the mathematical skills students will need to succeed in the workforce. DOL's workforce expertise underscored the value of ensuring that students have opportunities to understand how mathematical concepts are applied in real-world workplace settings and across a range of career pathways.
While the current priority already emphasizes evidence-based mathematics instruction and improved student achievement, we determined that it would be beneficial to more explicitly connect those academic foundations to workforce readiness. By encouraging engagement with national or regional employers to identify critical workplace mathematics skills and real-world applications, this addition will help ensure that mathematics instruction can both build strong academic foundations and demonstrate the relevance of those skills to future education, training, and employment opportunities. The revision therefore strengthens the connection between mathematics achievement and career preparation and better reflects the role that strong mathematics skills can play in preparing students for high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand occupations.
Current Priority:
The priority currently includes two parts focused on high-quality instructional materials (HQIM) in one or more specified subject areas: part (a)(ii) of the priority focuses on providing or expanding access to HQIM and part (a)(iii) focuses on providing or expanding access to training on implementing HQIM. Part (a)(iii) currently includes three parts.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to amend part (a)(ii)(1) and (a)(iii)(1) to expand the focus areas on STEM to include SI and cybersecurity. We also propose to add a new part (a)(ii)(2) and (a)(iii)(2) to include career and technical education programs of study, including programs integrating pre-apprenticeship and Registered Apprenticeship pathways, and to re-number the current (a)(ii)(2) and (a)(iii)(2) and succeeding parts in those paragraphs.
Reasons:
We are adding explicit references to SI and cybersecurity to emphasize these as critical components of STEM education and to incentivize the development and availability of HQIM in these subject areas. As SI becomes increasingly integrated across education, the workplace, and daily life,
(
printed page 69741)
students need access to high-quality instructional content that supports the development of foundational SI knowledge and skills and prepares them to engage with these technologies effectively. The added focus on cybersecurity reflects the importance of ensuring students have access to the high-quality instruction needed to meet evolving cybersecurity demands.
Additionally, we propose to include career and technical education programs of study under the HQIM paragraph to promote opportunities to strengthen the quality and rigor of these critical programs. This addition reflects, in particular, feedback from our partners at DOL, whose expertise in workforce development, apprenticeship, and career-connected learning led them to underscore the importance of ensuring that students participating in Career and Technical Education (CTE) have access to high-quality instructional content that prepares them for both continued education and employment. DOL also highlighted the value of creating stronger connections between classroom instruction and the skills students will need to succeed in the workplace, including through pre-apprenticeship and Registered Apprenticeship pathways.
Expanding the priority's focus on HQIM to expressly include CTE programs of study recognizes that high-quality instructional materials are important not only in traditional academic subjects, but also in career-connected learning. CTE programs increasingly integrate rigorous academic content, technical knowledge, hands-on learning, and preparation for industry-recognized credentials and further education and training. Specifically including these programs would encourage the development, adoption, and use of high-quality materials that strengthen the instructional foundation of CTE, better connect academic and technical learning, and help ensure that students are prepared to successfully transition from education into additional training, Registered Apprenticeship, or employment.
Together, these additions reflect feedback from our Federal partners and broaden the HQIM provision to better account for emerging instructional needs and the range of educational pathways through which students develop the knowledge and skills necessary for future success.
Current Priority:
Part (a)(v) focuses on creating and supporting implementation of strategic staffing models to incentivize educators and best leverage staffing in innovative ways to support student learning and achievement.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to amend part (a)(v) to expand the focus area on models for teacher and paraprofessional advancement to include Registered Apprenticeships.
Reasons:
We propose this change to explicitly promote Registered Apprenticeships as an innovative model for teacher and paraprofessional preparation and advancement. Feedback from our partners at DOL, drawing on expertise in apprenticeship and workforce development, highlighted the value of these structured, work-based pathways. Explicitly including Registered Apprenticeships would encourage approaches that combine related instruction with paid, on-the-job learning and create additional pathways for individuals to enter and advance in the education profession.
Current Priority:
Part (a) of the priority is focused on strengthening core instruction in several areas.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to add a new focus designated as part (a)(vii). This new proposed part will support professional development and technical assistance for local school board members and superintendents to improve student academic outcomes by establishing measurable outcome goals, using academic data to monitor progress, and incorporating regular monitoring of outcomes into local governance practices.
Reasons:
The decisions that local school board members and superintendents make about budgets, staffing, programs, and priorities have a significant impact on student academic outcomes. We propose to add this new focus on professional development and technical assistance to support them in their work and equip them with the knowledge and skills to interpret and use data about student academic outcomes.
Current Priority:
The current priority does not include text specific to student attendance and engagement.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to add a new part (f) focused on supporting students and families by implementing strategies to improve student attendance and engagement.
Reasons:
We propose this change to promote grant projects that address the critical challenge of student absenteeism and improve student attendance and engagement through approaches that support students and families. Feedback from our partners at HHS, drawing on their expertise serving children and families, reinforced the importance of addressing barriers that may contribute to absenteeism and disengagement. Explicitly including this focus in the priority will provide greater flexibility to support strategies that strengthen students' connection to school and help ensure they are present and engaged in learning.
Current Priority:
The current priority does not include text specific to building State and local capacity to strengthen governance with a focus on student outcomes.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to add a new part (g) that will focus on building State and local capacity to strengthen governance, including supporting locally elected school boards and superintendents in establishing and monitoring measurable academic outcomes.
Reasons:
Consistent with the previously mentioned proposed addition regarding professional development and technical assistance for local school board members and superintendents, we propose new part (g) to emphasize the need for building State and local capacity as it relates to governance centered around student outcomes. New part (g) will enable ED to leverage States to carry out this important work with the local leaders who govern their school systems.
Changes to Definitions
Current Definitions:
The current set of definitions finalized with the Secretary's Supplemental Priority on Meaningful Learning Opportunities does not include definitions of SI, pre-apprenticeship or Registered Apprenticeship.
Proposed Definitions:
We propose to add definitions of SI, pre-apprenticeship, and Registered Apprenticeship.
Reasons:
We propose to add definitions of these terms to support the revised priority proposed in this notice. The new definitions would apply to any use of these terms in the priority. Please see the earlier discussions of ED's rationale for proposing these specific definitions of SI, pre-apprenticeship, and Registered Apprenticeship.
Proposed Changes to the Notice of Final Priority and Definitions—Secretary's Supplemental Priority and Definitions on Career Pathways and Workforce Readiness (
91 FR 18780
)
Current Priority:
The current Career Pathways and Workforce Readiness priority addresses the key components of the career pathway continuum, with each component articulated as a distinct area of focus.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to add a new part (a) focused on the integration of activities across the full career pathway continuum to include a description of how the proposed
(
printed page 69742)
activities will be aligned to support students, workers, and jobseekers in accessing high-quality career pathways leading to high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand occupations.
Reasons:
Based on feedback from DOL, we identified an opportunity to build on the priority's existing focus on the key components of the career pathway continuum by more explicitly encouraging that those activities be intentionally connected and mutually reinforcing. This addition reflects DOL's workforce development expertise and emphasizes stronger alignment and transitions among education, training, and employment opportunities to support students, workers, and jobseekers as they progress toward high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand occupations.
Current Priority:
Part (a) supports workforce development programs aligned with State priorities and provides a comprehensive list of the activities that support those programs may include, such as alignment of workforce activities across State agencies, identifying credentials, providing support for trades and work-based learning opportunities and supporting pre-apprenticeships.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to redesignate the current part (a) to part (b) consistent with the proposed addition to this priority described immediately above. We propose to revise newly designated part (b) overall to expand (b)(i) to include the coordination of activities with local entities that support workforce development; add a new part (b)(ii) that focuses on coordinating activities with Tribal workforce priorities and with Tribes that support workforce development; and redesignating the proposed part (b)(ii) and succeeding paragraphs in this priority. In newly designated (b)(iii) (current part (a)(ii)) we propose to include a focus on aligning workforce activities among Tribes and local entities. We also propose to revise the text in the parenthetical to clarify that the examples are of entities that support workforce development, and we have added “career exploration” to the list of examples.
Reasons:
We propose these changes based on feedback from our Federal partners at DOL and DOI and their respective expertise in workforce development and Tribal education and workforce priorities. Feedback from DOL highlighted opportunities to strengthen coordination among State and local entities that support workforce development and to more expressly recognize career exploration as part of a comprehensive approach to preparing individuals for career pathways. Feedback from DOI identified opportunities to more expressly recognize Tribal workforce priorities and the role of Tribes and Tribal organizations in supporting workforce development. Together, these changes build on the priority's existing comprehensive approach by strengthening coordination across State, local, and Tribal workforce systems and better reflecting the range of entities that contribute to workforce development.
Current Priority:
Part (a)(iii) focuses on activities that support States in identifying in-demand and high value industry-recognized credentials and re-evaluating existing lists of credentials, and part (a)(vi) focuses on promoting the attainment of those same postsecondary credentials.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to redesignate these parts to (b)(iv) and (b)(vii) respectively, consistent with the proposed additions to this priority described previously. We propose to amend newly designated (b)(iv) and (b)(vii) to remove the modifiers of “in-demand and high-value” and instead use “high-quality” to describe the credentials that States should be identifying. Additionally, within newly designated (b)(iv), we propose to add the evaluation of credentials as an activity that would support States, expand settings in which such credentials may be identified, and support alignment of credentials across State education and workforce systems. In carrying out these activities, States would consider the Department of Labor's Training and Employment Notice (TEN) 04-26 as a resource for identifying approaches to evaluating and aligning credentials. We also propose to add aligning education and training programs with the high-quality industry-recognized credential identified.
Reasons:
Informed by feedback from DOL based on its expertise in workforce development and credential quality, we propose these changes to more clearly and consistently describe the credentials addressed by the priority. The changes also strengthen alignment with credentials already identified through State workforce systems and education and training programs, while recognizing the importance of evaluating credential quality and promoting greater consistency across education and workforce systems.
Current Priority:
Part (a)(v) focuses on the development of industry-led sector partnerships.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to redesignate this part to (b)(vi). In newly designated (b)(vi), we include development and expansion of partnerships with specific roles being laid out for employers to identify the in-demand skills and competencies, validate education and training models and credentials, and modify training based on hiring needs.
Reasons:
Based on feedback from DOL and its expertise in workforce development and industry-led sector partnerships, we identified an opportunity to build on the existing priority by supporting not only the development of new partnerships, but also the expansion of effective existing partnerships. We also propose to more clearly articulate the role of employers within these partnerships, including identifying in-demand skills and competencies, validating education and training models and credentials, and informing modifications to training based on hiring needs. These changes strengthen the connection between education and training programs and evolving workforce needs and help ensure that industry partnerships are meaningfully informed by employers.
Current Priority:
Current part (a)(viii) focuses on strategies to expand the availability of pre-apprenticeships and Registered Apprenticeships, including supporting apprenticeship intermediaries, Registered Apprenticeships for in-school and out-of-school youth, and providing technical assistance for states to advance these strategies.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to redesignate (a)(viii) to (b)(ix). Within the newly designated (b)(ix) we propose several revisions and additions. We propose to revise (b)(ix)(1) to clarify that we are referring to Registered Apprenticeships, and we propose to amend (b)(ix)(2) to include the expansion of pre-apprenticeships. Newly designated (b)(ix)(3) proposes to include the expansion of Registered Apprenticeship opportunities and proposes to add “adult learners” to the individuals who are identified as the beneficiaries of the apprenticeships described in this subpart. We propose to add a new part, (b)(ix)(4), to promote strategies to improve participant access, retention, completion, credential attainment, and employment outcomes for learners of all ages and redesignate the existing (b)(ix)(4) as (b)(ix)(5). Additionally, we propose to add (b)(ix)(6) to incorporate developing or strengthening partnerships among employers, labor-management organizations, industry associations, education and training providers, Registered Apprenticeship sponsorship, workforce development boards,
(
printed page 69743)
community-based organizations, and other partners to support the design, implementation, and scaling of Registered Apprenticeship programs; and we propose to add (b)(ix)(7) to promote the alignment of pre-apprenticeship and Registered Apprenticeship programs with industry-recognized credentials, postsecondary credit, career pathways, and supportive services to improve participant access, completion, and employment outcomes.
Reasons:
Based on feedback from DOL and its expertise in Registered Apprenticeship and workforce development, we identified opportunities to strengthen the priority's existing focus on pre-apprenticeships and Registered Apprenticeships by more expressly supporting the expansion of these opportunities and the partnerships necessary to sustain and scale them. These changes emphasize the importance of pre-apprenticeship programs that provide clear pathways into Registered Apprenticeship programs or other high-quality industry-recognized opportunities and strengthen alignment with established standards and practices in the field. The proposed changes to (b)(ix)(3) and the proposed addition of (b)(ix)(4) are intended to promote strategies for participant success for learners of all ages. The proposed changes also recognize the importance of expanding access to these opportunities for adult learners, including individuals seeking to enter or reenter the workforce, transition to new careers, or develop additional skills to advance in their current fields. By expressly including adult learners, the priority better reflects the role of pre-apprenticeships and Registered Apprenticeships in supporting lifelong learning, workforce participation, and economic mobility. The additions of (b)(ix)(6) and (b)(ix)(7) also recognize that successful apprenticeship pathways rely on intentional coordination among employers, labor-management organizations, industry associations, education and training providers, workforce development boards, community-based organizations, and other partners. More explicitly incorporating these partners and aligning apprenticeship opportunities with credentials, postsecondary credit, career pathways, and supportive services can strengthen the continuum from preparation and training to completion and employment.
Current Priority:
Part (a)(vii) discusses the provision of work-based learning opportunities and examples of such opportunities in which a student would receive wages or credit.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to redesignate this part to (b)(viii) consistent with the proposed additions to this priority described previously. We propose to specify that the opportunities should be qualified by being high-skill, high-wage or within an in-demand industry sector or occupation.
Reasons:
Based on feedback from DOL, informed by its expertise in workforce development and labor market needs, we propose these changes to strengthen the connection between work-based learning and meaningful employment opportunities. Emphasizing opportunities in high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand industry sectors or occupations would help ensure that work-based learning provides students with relevant workplace experience and skills that support successful transitions into employment and continued career advancement.
Current Priority:
Part (b) of the Career Pathways and Workforce readiness priority is focused on the need for awareness of the range of postsecondary educational and career options.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to redesignate this part to part (c) consistent with the proposed additions to this priority described previously. And, we propose to amend the language in part (c) to include career and college navigation, coaching, and supportive services to promote greater awareness of the range of postsecondary educational and career options, including employment outcomes and earnings, of the students that pursue each of these options.
Reasons:
Based on feedback from DOL and its expertise in workforce development and career pathways, we identified an opportunity to build on the priority's existing focus on awareness of postsecondary education and career options by more clearly identifying the types of navigation, coaching, exploration, advising, and support that can help students understand and pursue those options. DOL's feedback also highlighted the value of providing students with information about employment outcomes, including earnings, to strengthen the connection between education and career decision-making and help students make informed choices about pathways that lead to education, training, and employment opportunities.
Current Priority:
The current priority does not include a specific mention of support for workforce-readiness activities and in identifying those activities in the field.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to add a part (d) to support workforce readiness activities, including employability skills, digital literacy, SI literacy, financial literacy, resume and interview preparation, job search assistance, workplace expectations, decision-making skills, and other skills needed to obtain and retain employment in high-skill, high-wage, or in-demand occupations.
Reasons:
Based on feedback from DOL and its expertise in preparing individuals to enter and succeed in the workforce, we identified an opportunity to more expressly recognize workforce-readiness activities within the priority. While the priority already addresses a range of activities that connect education and training to employment, this addition more clearly reflects the foundational skills and supports that can help individuals successfully obtain and retain employment. Specifically identifying activities such as employability skills, digital and financial literacy, SI literacy, job-search preparation, understanding workplace expectations, and decision-making skills also strengthens alignment between ED's career pathways efforts and workforce development practices in the field and demonstrates readiness for work in an SI-driven economy.
Current Priority:
Part (e)(iii)(2) focuses on creating targeted pathways for instructional assistants, paraprofessionals, substitute teachers, and other such positions, and allowing them to earn credentials.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to redesignate this part to (g)(iii)(2) consistent with the proposed additions to this priority described previously. We propose to include language at the end of this part that includes Registered Apprenticeship programs as a specific type of pathway.
Reasons:
Based on consultation with DOL and its expertise in Registered Apprenticeship programs, we identified an opportunity to more explicitly recognize Registered Apprenticeships as a pathway for instructional assistants, paraprofessionals, substitute teachers, and individuals in similar positions to earn credentials and advance within the education profession. This addition highlights the applicability of the Registered Apprenticeship model within the education workforce and provides greater specificity regarding how the pathways already contemplated under the priority may be implemented.
Current Priority:
The priority did not address alignment of Registered Apprenticeship programs with education preparation programs, State certification or licensure requirements.
(
printed page 69744)
It also did not address supports, including mentoring and coaching.
Proposed Priority:
We propose adding a new part (g)(iii)(6) and a part (g)(iii)(7). Proposed part (g)(iii)(6) would incorporate supporting articulation, credit transfer, or other alignment between educator Registered Apprenticeship programs, educator preparation programs, and State certification or licensure requirements. Proposed part (g)(iii)(7) incorporates developing or expanding supports for apprentices in educator Registered Apprenticeship programs, such as mentoring, coaching, academic support, exam preparation, or other services that support completion and certification.
Reasons:
Based on consultation with DOL and its expertise in Registered Apprenticeship programs, we identified opportunities to strengthen the priority's support for successful educator Registered Apprenticeships. In particular, DOL's feedback highlighted the importance of connecting Registered Apprenticeship programs with educator preparation programs and State certification or licensure requirements, as well as providing apprentices with supports that facilitate successful completion. Proposed parts (6) and (7) more expressly recognize these elements by supporting alignment and articulation across programs and requirements and by identifying mentoring, coaching, academic support, exam preparation, and other services that can help apprentices progress through the pathway, complete their program, and obtain the credentials necessary to enter the profession.
Changes to Definitions
Current Definitions:
The current set of definitions finalized with the Secretary's Supplemental Priority on Career Pathways and Workforce Readiness does not include definitions of pre-apprenticeship, Registered Apprenticeship, SI, or SI literacy.
Proposed Definitions:
We propose to add definitions of pre-apprenticeship, Registered Apprenticeship, SI, and SI literacy.
Reasons:
We propose to add definitions of these terms to support the revised priority proposed in this notice. The new definitions would apply to all uses of the terms in the Secretary's Supplemental Priority on Career Pathways and Workforce Readiness. Please see the earlier discussion of ED's rationale for proposing these definitions of pre-apprenticeship and Registered Apprenticeship.
See our previous discussions about the terms pre-apprenticeship, Registered Apprenticeship, SI, and SI literacy for more information about the basis of these definitions.
Current Definition:
The definition of Learning and Employment Record (LER) finalized with the Secretary's Supplemental Priority on Career Pathways and Workforce Readiness does not include any descriptors for operationalizing the definition. Additionally, the definition of Skills-Based Job Description Generator incorrectly repeats the definition of Learning and Employment Record.
Proposed Definition:
We are proposing to revise the definition of Learning and Employment Record to include these necessary descriptors, and we are proposing a new definition of Skills-Based Job Description Generator that correctly reflects our intended definition.
Reasons:
The revised definitions of Learning and Employment Record and Skills-Based Job Description generator describe these terms as more than a digital tool and explain more thoroughly the meaning and essence of each.
Proposed Changes to the Notice of Final Priority and Definitions—Secretary's Supplemental Priority and Definitions on Advancing Artificial Intelligence in Education (
91 FR 18774
)
Current Priority:
Part (a)(vii) is focused on partnering with State educational agencies or local educational agencies in the offering of dual-enrollment course opportunities.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to amend subpart (vii) of part (a) to include Tribal education agencies and Tribal organizations (as defined in
20 U.S.C. 7452(b)(3)
and
25 U.S.C. 5304(l)
respectively) along with State education agencies and local educational agencies.
Reasons:
We propose this change to ensure that the priority appropriately recognizes the role of Tribal education agencies and Tribal organizations in expanding access to dual-enrollment opportunities. In considering feedback from Federal partners at DOI, including their expertise in Tribal education, and through Tribal consultation on grants-related issues, we identified an opportunity to more expressly reflect Tribal organizations throughout the priorities. Adding Tribal education agencies and Tribal organizations to this provision clarifies that partnerships to expand dual-enrollment opportunities may include these entities and better reflects the range of education partners that can support students' access to postsecondary coursework and pathways.
Current Priority:
The priority includes two parts, (a) and (b). Part (a) provides 11 subparts, (i) through (xi), that speak to the expansion of the understanding of AI in education.
Proposed Priority:
In addition to the earlier discussion about proposed changes to the terms and definitions of SI and SI literacy, we propose adding a subpart (viii) to part (a) that addresses partnering with employers or industry associations to develop educational materials and training programs that provide industry or occupational specific SI literacy and further SI skills development. Additionally, we propose to redesignate the current subpart (viii) and succeeding subparts of part (a) to conform with the numbering of this proposed subpart.
Reasons:
We propose this addition based on feedback received through our continued partnership with DOL. Drawing on its expertise in workforce development and engagement with employers and industry, DOL identified an opportunity to strengthen the priority by more explicitly connecting SI literacy and skills development with the needs of specific industries and occupations. This revision highlights the value of engaging employers and industry associations in developing educational materials and training programs so that students can develop SI skills relevant to evolving workplace needs. This addition also advances the goals of the President's Executive Order on
Advancing Artificial Intelligence Education for American Youth,
Exec. Order No. 14277,
90 FR 17519
(April 28, 2025), including its emphasis on equipping students with the skills necessary to use and create the next generation of AI technology and preparing them for an AI-enabled workforce.
Current Priority:
There are 11 subparts under part (a). Each of the 11 subparts discusses AI literacy with one or more specific focus areas.
Proposed Priority:
We propose adding a subpart (ix) to promote SI literacy efforts aligned with the five content areas and seven delivery principles outlined within the DOL's February 13, 2026 AI Literacy Framework (Notice 07-25), and redesignate the succeeding subparts accordingly. See the previous discussion for maintaining use of the term AI in reference to DOL's AI Literacy Framework.
Additionally, we propose to redesignate the current subpart (ix) and succeeding subparts of part (a) to conform with the numbering of this proposed subpart.
Reasons:
We propose this addition to reflect ED's continued coordination with DOL on efforts to strengthen SI literacy and prepare learners for an increasingly SI-enabled workforce.
(
printed page 69745)
DOL's February 13, 2026 AI Literacy Framework (Notice 07-25) provides a common structure for SI literacy through five content areas and seven delivery principles that can help connect education and workforce preparation. Referencing the Framework in this priority will promote greater alignment across Federal SI literacy efforts and provide applicants with a useful framework for designing activities that build relevant SI knowledge and skills, while preserving flexibility in how those activities are implemented.
Current Priority:
There are 11 subparts in part (b). Each of the subparts supports a specific focus area or population.
Proposed Priority:
We propose adding a new subpart (b)(iv) that would support SI projects that are designed for all students, and redesignating the succeeding paragraphs as appropriate.
Reasons:
Through consultation with our Federal partners, we identified the value of maintaining specific focus areas while also providing a broader option that can be applied across programs and student populations, where appropriate. While the existing subparts identify important populations and areas of focus, SI-related projects may also present opportunities that are not limited to a particular population or educational context. Adding this subpart would provide greater flexibility to support innovative SI projects designed to benefit all students, while retaining the more targeted focus areas for programs where those approaches are most appropriate.
Current Priority:
The current part (b) does not explicitly name evidence-building around SI in education and does not address developing and disseminating evidence-informed frameworks, tools, or models for integrating SI into education.
Proposed Priority:
We propose adding two new subparts, (b)(xii) and (b)(xiii) to support evidence-building for projects advancing SI in education, and to support developing and disseminating evidence-informed frameworks, tools, and models for integrating SI into education.
Reasons:
Based on ED's experience implementing this priority during FY 2026, we identified additional opportunities to expand the types of SI in education projects that may be supported. In particular, implementation highlighted the value of supporting projects that build the evidence base on whether and how SI-enabled approaches improve student outcomes or other relevant outcomes, consistent with applicable statutory and regulatory standards for evidence. We also identified an opportunity to support the development and dissemination of evidence-informed frameworks, tools, and models that can help students, teachers, educators, administrators, and service providers apply emerging evidence when integrating SI into education. These additions would expand the priority to support both the development of evidence and its translation into practical resources for educational settings.
Current Priority:
Part (b)(xi) focuses on using technology to improve program outcomes.
Proposed Priority:
We propose to redesignate this part to (b)(xiv). Additionally, we propose to amend (b)(xiv) by adding a rigorous and specific deployment of the technology in teaching methods or student supports.
Reasons:
The existing language provides broad flexibility to support the use of technology to improve program outcomes. We propose this amendment to provide greater specificity regarding the use of SI in teaching methods and student supports and to emphasize rigorous and purposeful deployment. As SI becomes increasingly relevant in educational settings, this additional specificity will help focus projects on well-designed applications of SI that are responsive to identified needs and support improved program and student outcomes.

Types of Priorities
When inviting applications for a competition using one or more priorities, we designate the type of each priority as absolute, competitive preference, or invitational through a notice in the
Federal Register
. The effect of each type of priority follows:
Absolute priority:
Under an absolute priority, we consider only applications that meet the priority (
34 CFR 75.105(c)(3)
).
Competitive preference priority:
Under a competitive preference priority, we give competitive preference to an application by (1) awarding additional points, depending on the extent to which the application meets the priority (
34 CFR 75.105(c)(2)(i)
); or (2) selecting an application that meets the priority over an application of comparable merit that does not meet the priority (
34 CFR 75.105(c)(2)(ii)
).
Invitational priority:
Under an invitational priority, we are particularly interested in applications that meet the priority. However, we do not give an application that meets the priority a preference over other applications (
34 CFR 75.105(c)(1)
).

Proposed Definitions for Proposed Priorities on Promoting Evidence-Based Literacy, Expanding Education Choice, and Returning Education to the States
Computer science
means the study of computers and algorithmic processes, including their principles, their hardware and software designs, theories, computational thinking, coding, analytics, applications, and super intelligence (SI).
Computer science often includes computer programming or coding as a tool to create software, including applications, games, websites, and tools to manage or manipulate data; or development and management of computer hardware and the other electronics related to sharing, securing, and using digital information. In addition to coding, the expanding field of computer science emphasizes computational thinking and interdisciplinary problem-solving to equip students with the skills and abilities necessary to apply computation to the digital world.
Computer science does not involve using computers for everyday tasks, such as browsing the internet or using tools like word processors, spreadsheets, or presentation software. Instead, it focuses on creating and developing technology, not just utilizing it.
Evidence framework
means an approach to providing a determination about whether an activity, strategy, or intervention meets each aspect of the definition of strong evidence or moderate evidence (as defined in
20 U.S.C. 7801(21)(A)(i)
(I-II)), as applicable.
(a) An evidence framework must include each of the following:
(i) Whether or not a study is an experimental study or quasi-experimental design study;
(ii) Whether or not a study shows a positive, statistically significant effect on student outcomes or other relevant outcomes;
(iii) Whether or not a study uses outcome measures that demonstrate validity and reliability, that do not give an unfair advantage to participants in one condition over another, and that are measured consistently for the groups or participants that are being compared;
(iv) Whether or not a study design is otherwise of high quality, including whether it minimizes factors outside the intervention that could affect student or other relevant outcomes (confounds) and whether random assignment (if used) was done with integrity; and
(v) Whether or not study implementation and analysis is appropriate, including whether groups or participants being compared demonstrate baseline equivalence on key individual and other relevant characteristics, whether differences in baseline equivalence are statistically controlled, and by considering the impact on the validity of the study of any changes to the sample over time.
(b) An evidence framework may be implemented or verified by one or more of the following:
(i) An organization with relevant expertise that has demonstrated to the Department that it has a rigorous, transparent (
i.e.,
publicly accessible) process for determining each aspect identified in (a).
(ii) By peer reviewers with statistical expertise who apply an evidence framework consistent with each aspect identified in (a) in reviewing support for an applicant's assertion that relevant information is strong evidence or moderate evidence, as applicable.
(iii) By the Department or peer reviewers with statistical expertise who affirm an applicant's assertion that relevant information is strong evidence or moderate evidence because it is supported by study ratings included in the What Works Clearinghouse in one or more of:
(1) A practice guide.
(2) An intervention report.
(3) Individual studies otherwise assessed to meet strong evidence or moderate evidence.
Evidence-based literacy instruction
means literacy instruction that relates to
(
printed page 69748)
explicit, systematic and intentional instruction in phonological awareness, phonic decoding, oral and sign language, vocabulary, language structure, reading fluency, reading comprehension, and writing; promotes knowledge-rich materials; and is backed by one or more of the following, as supported by an evidence framework (as defined in this notice):
(a) Strong evidence, meaning an activity, strategy, or intervention that demonstrates a statistically significant effect on improving student outcomes or other relevant outcomes based on at least one well-designed and well-implemented experimental study (strong evidence as defined in
20 U.S.C. 7801(21)(A)(i)(I)
).
(b) Moderate evidence, meaning an activity, strategy, or intervention that demonstrates a statistically significant effect on improving student outcomes or other relevant outcomes based on at least one well-designed and well-implemented quasi-experimental study (moderate evidence as defined in
20 U.S.C. 7801(21)(A)(i)(II)
).
Note:
In any discretionary grant program competition in which the definition of “evidence-based literacy instruction” is used as proposed, the Secretary may use the entire definition or one or more of the subparts of the definition that are most relevant for the grant program competition.
Experimental study
means a study that is designed to compare outcomes between two groups (such as students) that are otherwise equivalent except for their assignment to either a treatment group receiving an activity, strategy, intervention, process, product, practice, or policy as compared with a control group that does not. Experimental studies can support claims of strong evidence. Randomized controlled trials and single-case design studies are specific types of experimental studies that meet this definition.
Pre-apprenticeship
means a program designed to prepare individuals to enter and succeed in one or more Registered Apprenticeship programs, consistent with the elements of pre-apprenticeship established under
20 CFR 681.480
and informed by the U.S. Department of Labor's Framework for Effective Pre-Apprenticeships in Training and Employment Notice No. 05-26. An effective pre-apprenticeship provides direct pathways into Registered Apprenticeship programs through defined agreements with Registered Apprenticeship sponsors; industry-driven training and curriculum aligned with Registered Apprenticeship standards; hands-on, meaningful work-based learning and career exposure; access to educational and career counseling and other supportive services through broad workforce and education partnerships that leverage available resources; and strategies for tracking participant outcomes and supporting continuous program improvement.
Quasi-experimental design study
means a study using a design that attempts to approximate an experimental study by identifying a comparison group that is similar to the treatment group in important respects. Cross-sectional group designs, comparative interrupted time series, difference-in-difference designs, and growth curve designs are specific types of quasi-experimental studies that meet this definition. This type of study can meet the definition of moderate evidence but not strong evidence.
Recognized postsecondary credential
means a credential consisting of an industry-recognized certificate or certification, a certificate of completion of an apprenticeship, a license recognized by the State involved or Federal Government, or an associate or baccalaureate degree, as defined in section 3(52) of the Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act.
Registered Apprenticeship
means an apprenticeship program that meets the national standards for apprenticeship established under
29 U.S.C. Chapter 4C
(the National Apprenticeship Act) and
29 CFR parts 29
and
30
and is registered with the U.S. Department of Labor's Office of Apprenticeship or a recognized State Apprenticeship Agency. A Registered Apprenticeship combines on-the-job learning with related technical instruction, provides progressive wage increases tied to demonstrated competency, and results in a nationally recognized credential awarded upon completion.
Talent marketplace
means a digital, interconnected system of technologies maintained by a State or State Workforce Agency, as defined at
29 U.S.C. 3225a(a)(8)
, that
(a) is publicly available;
(b) includes an integrated:
(i) Learning and Employment Record;
(ii) Credential Registry; and
(iii) Skill-Based Job Description generator;
(c) utilizes super intelligence to enable learners and jobseekers, employers, and education and training providers to transform, transcribe, and transact earned learning assertions, job descriptions, and degree and non-degree credentials into discrete competency statements; and
(d) may be curated into interoperable individual records of achievement and learning and employment recommendations.
Super intelligence
(SI) means the technologies and systems encompassed by the term “artificial intelligence” as defined in
15 U.S.C. 9401(3)
.
SI Literacy
means the technical knowledge, durable skills, civic awareness, and future ready attitudes, including SI related ethical reasoning, critical social inquiry, interdisciplinary problem-solving, and creativity, required to thrive in a world influenced by SI. It enables learners to understand how SI works; use SI tools effectively and responsibly; engage, create with, manage, and design SI, while critically evaluating its benefits, risks, and implications.
